Question: Can I get into a top graduate school for computer science with a 3.6 GPA? What schools would I be eligible for? (I have a decent amount of research experience but all of my research is applying CS to other topics)
Answer: Every top computer science graduate school regularly admits applicants with 3.6 GPAs. Your GPA definitely won’t get you into a top computer science graduate school, because that’s not how anyone gets in, but it won’t keep you out either. Here’s some real data from my own CS department, which has been ranked #5 in the country by US News for more than 20 years. We received more than 1450 applicants for Fall 2023 admission to our PhD program. I sorted these by normalized undergraduate GPA—breaking ties randomly—and partitioned them into 100-student cohorts. Here are GPA ranges and numbers of admission offers for the top 12 cohorts, plus a 13th “cohort” for all lower GPAs. (Yes, we got more than 100 applications with perfect 4.00 GPAs, and yes, we rejected most of them.) All else being equal, a typical applicant with a 3.6 GPA had about 13% chance of admission. For comparison, our overall PhD admission rate this year was about 17%. But of course, not all else is equal. Admissions committees are looking primarily for concrete evidence of research potential. Your research experience should increase your chances, especially if your statement or purpose describes your research efforts in the fluent technical language of active researchers (as opposed to starry-eyed but uninformed “passion”), and you have supportive letters of recommendation that describe your research efforts in credible, technical, and personal detail. The fact that your experience is all in “applying CS to other topics” is not a problem; with the right spin, your expertise outside CS could be sold as a significant advantage.

Question: Can one's own conference paper be published in a journal, if it has already been published in a conference?
Answer: This varies significantly by field (and subfield). But for computer science, the short answer is yes, with caveats. In computer science, most research papers are published first in conference proceedings. Some of conference papers are later republished in journals, with significant new content added. Specifics vary from journal to journal, but as a general rule of thumb, at least 30ish% of the journal paper should be new. It’s important to note that the 30% rule doesn’t describe words, but substance. A journal version that simply uses half again as many words to report exactly the same results as a conference paper could be reasonably rejected. On the other hand, a journal version that uses new ideas to obtain shorter proofs of theoretical results in a conference paper could be reasonably accepted. In more theoretical subfields, the new content can consist entirely of complete proofs, as opposed to the sketches that usually appear in conference papers, but new results are not generally required. If a theory conference paper already contains complete proofs, some theory journals do not require any novel content, even when the paper is not invited, but others do, even when the paper is invited. (Cue angry arguments over whether conference papers with electronic proceedings should have page limits.) The journal version must also explicitly cite the previous conference version, and the new content in the journal version should be explicitly spelled out in the cover letter, if not in the paper itself. See, for example, the official ACM journal policies, which require 25% new content by default, but also note that the requirement is subjective and that invited journal papers may be exempt from the novelty requirement. tl;dr: Read the submission rules for the journal and follow them. The “30% new content” guideline applies only to sending extended versions of conference papers to journals. With rare exceptions, you cannot send an extended version of a paper from conference X to conference Y, or an extended version of a paper from journal 1 to journal 2. Finally, at least in my opinion, honesty requires considering the conference and journal papers as two versions of the same paper, not as two independent papers. In particular, all versions of the same paper should have exactly the same title, and the paper should appear as a single item in your CV, citing all publication venues—technical report, arXiv, conference, and journal, for example. .

Question: If you need to publish an academic paper in a journal, which database is more important to you for the journal to be indexed in, PubMed or WoS?
Answer: [A2A] Neither. I’ve never cared and it’s never mattered. Why should anyone care about what some company thinks? I’m a named full professor in a top-5 department in a top-10 engineering college. I have almost two decades of experience on faculty hiring committees and more than an decade of experience on promotions and tenure committees, at both the department and college levels. When I write that it’s never mattered, I don’t just mean that it’s never mattered for my career; I also mean it’s never mattered in the hundreds of hiring and promotion cases that I’ve helped to evaluate. I don’t recall a single committee I’ve been on ever querying PubMed, WoS/ISI, or Scopus to check the legitimacy of a publication venue. Instead, the primary consideration is whether the work is actually good. (Many papers in top venues are not actually good; many actually good papers are not published in top venues.) A distant second consideration is whether the publication venue has a good reputation within the research community. (Some indexed venues have bad reputations; some venues with good reputations aren’t indexed.) Moreover, these considerations are applied to the candidate’s entire body of work, not to individual papers. Does the candidate’s research community consider the candidate’s work, in the aggregate, to be actually good? Is the candidate’s work, in the aggregate, published in venues with good reputations? In short: Do the best research you can. Write the best papers you can. For each paper, aim for the venue most likely to reach that paper’s intended audience, taking into account both the scope of the venue (meaning the interests of the venue’s readers) and the paper’s chances of acceptance. If your university has a rule about publications only counting if they appear in venues indexed by X, then yeah, you need to publish in a venue indexed by X. It’s a weird rule, but still, you need to know it and follow it.

Question: Why do mathematicians believe in the truth of ridiculous vacuous statements such as "all unicorns are green"?
Answer: It’s not ridiculous! It’s the only thing that makes sense! It might be easier to see that the negation of this sentence must be false. De Morgan’s law implies that the following formulas are logically equivalent: In particular, if X is the set of unicorns, and P is the property of being green, we get an equivalence between two sentences: These two sentences have exactly the same meaning. The second sentence is clearly false, because there are no unicorns at all. Thus, the first sentence is also false. Because it’s the same sentence. I suspect the source of your discomfort isn’t really about the vacuous quantifier, but about the definition of implication. The operator p → q (read “ p implies q ” or “if p then q ”) is defined as the boolean function with the following truth table: p q p → q T T T T F F F T T F F T In other words, the expression p → q has exactly the same meaning as the expression ¬ p ∨ q , For example: “If you oversleep, then you will miss your flight” means exactly the same thing as “Don’t oversleep, or you will miss your flight”. This definition has a powerful but counterintuitive consequence: If the hypothesis p is false, then the implication p → q is true. In normal conversational English, we use “if…then…” to express causal relationships: If you oversleep, then because you overslept you will miss your flight. We sometimes also informally use “if…then…” to express logical equivalence: The sentence “If you oversleep, then you will miss your flight” might suggest that the oversleeping is the only way to miss your flight. But in formal propositional logic, implication doesn’t say anything at all about cause, and it doesn’t express equivalence. The implication “If you oversleep, then you will miss your flight” remains true even if you wake up on time and you miss your flight (for example, because your Uber gets a flat tire). Now consider the implication “If George is a unicorn, then George is green.” We know that George is not a unicorn, because unicorns don’t exist. So by definition, the implication is true! Moreover, it’s true for every George! As Alon writes in his answer, it is possible to formulate the rules of logic to make explicit exceptions for the empty set. And indeed, the earliest formalizations of set theory did exactly that! Early set theorists really did not consider sets without elements to be well-defined objects. Eventually they conceded the existence of the empty set, as a well-defined set, as a matter of convenience. In hindsight, formulating logic without the empty set makes just as much sense (at least to me) as formulating the rules of arithmetic without zero. Yeah, you can do that if you really really really had to, but it’s so much more convenient to let zero be an integer. Why feel weird about zero being even? it’s twice an integer isn’t it? Why not let the answer to “How many people are in the room?” be an integer, even when the room is empty? Why be confused when the number of unicorns equals the number of green unicorns?

Question: What are some free online sites where you can submit your journal papers in computer science for publication after acceptance from international conferences and journals?
Answer: The best option is the journal or conference proceedings itself. An increasing number of conferences and journals are open access, and in particular diamond open access, meaning authors do not pay a fee to publish papers, and readers do not pay a fee to read papers. Instead, the low cost of maintaining the database of papers is covered by volunteer labor (just like reviewing and editing everywhere), donations, grants, and a small increment in conference registration fees. (In particular, publication venues that build on top of arXiv rely on arXiv’s funding.) For most publishers like ACM, IEEE, and Springer, diamond open access isn’t an option. By default, authors do not have to pay a fee to publish with these companies (except for conferences, where at least one author must pay the conference registration fee), but readers must either have a subscription (often through their university library or their company) or pay a fee to read each paper. Many of these publishers make their content open-access after an embargo period, which can range from 12 mohths to 5 years. But thanks in part to open-access mandates from funding agencies, you can still publish open-access versions of papers accepted to non-open-access venues at arXiv or other similar preprint/archive servers. Google Scholar indexes not only every major commercial and open-access publisher, but also arXiv and several other open-access repositories (including HAL, Zenodo, and several institutional servers). In particular, Scholar tracks citations between papers on all these platforms. (People who think citations from unrefereed papers shouldn’t count are weird.) You also have the option of simply publishing a preprint version of the paper on your own professional web site. Google Scholar might still discover and index your paper, especially if your web site’s URL uses the “.edu” top-level domain, but you can always update your own Google Scholar profile manually to make sure your papers are indexed.

Question: As someone starting with machine learning with a background in some programming topics (OOP, Problem-solving, DSA) how can I come up with an idea for a research paper or project (AI related) that is worth participating in some amateur conference?
Answer: Read LOTS of papers. Think about questions that those papers should have answered but didn’t. (Well-written papers will openly state such questions, under the heading of “open problems” or “directions for future research”.) At the same time, talk with LOTS of other people who work on topics that you find interesting. (One way to do this is to go to conferences. Yes, even when you don’t have a paper. No, strike that—especially when you don’t have a paper.) Ask them about questions that they feel like they should be able to answer but can’t. Pick one of those questions that you find interesting. Make substantial progress toward an answer. Write a paper (or a poster) describing your results. Keep in mind that conferences generally do not accept “ideas” or “topics” or “questions”. They accept results, and more specifically, well-written presentations of results. But your first goal is to find interesting things to work on.

Question: What is a systematic approach to come up with a research topic that can be published in a top CS conference?
Answer: You’re asking the wrong question. Research topics aren’t published in top CS conferences. Research results are published in top CS conferences. (Strictly speaking, even that’s not correct—research papers are published in top CS conferences. But those papers are judged primarily on the strength and novelty of their results. It’s not enough to be about a relevant and interesting topic.) But the answer is still NO. If anyone knew of a truly systematic approach to develop research results that would be published in a top CS conference, that approach would quickly be automated, the resulting software would be used to flood that conference with results, and the conference would be ruined for mere humans. In short, that particular research area would be driven into irrelevant oblivion; researchers would move on to more interesting topics.

Question: If a scientific experiment that is extremely important, costs too much to be conducted, say 2.5-3 million dollars who or what is at fault? The scientific community for being too expensive or the person incapable of affording it?
Answer: “Fault” implies that someone did something wrong, but nothing wrong is happening here. Even if something wrong were happening, “fault” is rarely a useful framing. “Experimenter X does not have the necessary resources to carry out experiment Y.” is neither a criticism of experimenter X nor a criticism of experiment Y. This is just a fact, like “Peggy isn’t old enough to get a driver’s license.” or “Johnny is allergic to peanuts.” or “I have less money than Elon Musk.” However, if experimenter X insists that Y is the only experiment that they are willing (or able, or eager) to perform, even though they don’t have the necessary resources to perform it, that is a choice by experimenter X. Similarly, if experimenter X refuses to apply for additional funding to support experiment Y, even though reasonable opportunities for such funding exist, that is a choice by experimenter X. And those choices may have serious and unpleasant consequences, like failure to get tenure. Experimenter X is responsible for those choices. Symmetrically, if department Z insists that experimenter X perform experiment Y, even though X cannot (despite good-faith effort) obtain the necessary resources to perform Y, that is a choice by department Z. And that choice may have serious and unpleasant consequences, like losing experimenter X. Department Z is responsible for that choice. Reality is rarely this simple. Real-world situations involve complex mixtures of choices and responsibilities. Assigning “fault” for unpleasant events to a single actor is unlikely to be helpful (or even honest), because it completely ignores this complexity.

Name: Jeff Erickson
Question: Can we assume that there exists a possibility that P = NP = PSPACE, given that the paper on P = NP = PSPACE has not been rejected yet by Journal of the ACM, which had been rejected within two months in previous submissions?
Answer: [A2A] If you have a proof that P = NP = PSPACE, then P = NP = PSPACE, not as a “possibility”, but as a certainty. That’s what a proof means. Similarly, if you have a proof that P ≠ NP, then P ≠ NP, and if you have a proof that NP ≠ PSPACE, then NP ≠ PSPACE. In either of these cases, there is abslutely no possibility that P = NP = PSPACE. Again, that’s what a proof means. Without one of these proofs, we just don’t know whether P = NP = PSPACE. It might be true; it might be false. Most experts believe all three classes are distinct, and there are good heuristic arguments for that stance, but belief is not certainty, and heuristic arguments are not a proof. So we’re in a weird situation. On one hand, you’ve submitted a paper called “P = NP = PSPACE” to JACM, which presumably contains a proof (since otherwise you don’t have anything to submit), which means you’re convinced that P = NP = PSPACE. On the other hand, you are asking about whether it is possible for P = NP = PSPACE, which means you aren’t convinced that P = NP = PSPACE. So which is it? Do you have a proof or don’t you? I’ll give you a hint: You don’t. Because if you did, you would have already posted your complete proof on the open web (carefully avoiding well-known pitfalls and crank indicators), you would already be giving talks about your proof around the world, complexity experts would have already tried and failed to find an error, and the research community would be losing its collective minds. The fact that you have not posted your complete proof for public scrutiny already makes me suspicious. But at least you’ve posted a screenshot of your first page. Unfortunately, I see crank indicators already in the abstract. Why are you considering Graph Isomorphism separately? It’s well known that GI is in NP, so any proof that P=NP immediately implies that GI is in P. The abstract is full of unexplained notation (What does φ ( a | b ) mean?) and terminology (What does “properly disjoint” mean?). What on earth is “the syntax of the satisfiability of a 3SAT problem”? (That one could be an artifact of weak English fluency, but that’s a poor excuse. Given the importance of your claimed result, you should be moving heaven and earth to make sure the English of your abstract is absolutely flawless. Or at least, you should post a reference version in your native language.) This looks more like private notes to yourself than a document written for other people to read. That’s enough to convince me that I don’t want to spend any more time thinking about your “proof”; I’ll stick to my default expectation that it’s wrong. I’ll change my mind if a well-known expert like Avi Widgerson or Scott Aaronson publicly endorses your argument, but until then, I’m done.

Name: Jeff Erickson
Question: How can I find out if a research paper I've posted to arXiv has gotten any references?
Answer: The most useful tool I know of for tracking citations, especially for arXiv preprints, is Google Scholar. ArXiv preprints are usually indexed within a few days of their release, so you can find a record for your preprint either in your own profile or by searching for the title. Each paper on your own profile is listed with the number of citations that Google has discovered; that number is a link to a page with a bar chart showing when the paper was cited. From there, or from a title search, you can click on the “cited by ##” link to find a list of the papers that cited yours. If you don’t have a Google Scholar profile yet, you can set one up in a few minutes. You can also add papers directly to your profile, but it will take a few days for them to be properly indexed. Google Scholar has some significant flaws; the fact that it indexes unrefereed papers (and citations from unrefereed papers) is not one of them. In particular, at least for computer science, it is significantly more reliable than commercial citation services like Scopus or Web of Science, which ignore arXiv preprints entirely. It also has the advantage of being free. I do not work for Google. On the other hand, I have spent decades on various faculty hiring and promotion committees, and we’ve always used Google Scholar to get citation counts. On the gripping hand, citation counts are at best an extremely crude proxy for visibility and impact. If you’re worried about whether people are seeing your research, your time is better spent on marketing than on Scholar-stalking. Send your paper to people who you genuinely think would be interested. Give seminar talks about your work, both within your own department and elsewhere. Go to relevant conferences and talk about your work—not just in talks, but at coffee breaks, lunch, or anytime anyone asks what you’re working on.

Answer: First of all, no, I can’t give you a research title for research that hasn’t been done yet, because titles describe research that has already been done. First do the research; then choose a title that concisely describes your results. Second… You really can’t think of anything? Really? Nothing? None of your classes discussed the limits of knowledge in your field? None of the other papers you’ve read suggested open problems or directions for further research? You’ve never tossed around half-baked ideas with your professors and other colleagues? You’re not actively curious about anything? It sounds like you need to build up your background and develop some actual research interests. Most active researchers have no trouble finding research that nobody’s done before. The real hurdle is finding open research problems where you have a thorough understanding of the state of the art; you have a good idea of how to make progress; you have the necessary resources (especially time and expertise) to carry out the work; you actually care about the result; and you have good reason to believe that the research community will care about the result. In short, the hard part is finding a research problem where you can realistically make progress. The only way to get better at finding problems to work on is to work closely with people who know you and whose interests are reasonably close to your own. Graduate students typically call these people advisors. Strangers on the internet can’t help you, because we don’t know you.

Question: In the introduction section of my research paper, can I write my own background based on my knowledge of the topic, or do I have to rely on what other researchers have said?
Answer: Both!! Almost by definition, everything you write is based on your own knowledge of the topic. That’s what writing is—communicating your knowledge to other people. On the other hand, your readers have no reason to trust you You need to convince them that you know what you’re talking about. You need to justify any claims you make, even in the introduction, either by direct reasoning (based on premises that must be justified, recursively) or by citing the appropriate literature. You also need to give proper credit for any ideas or results or techniques you describe, even in the introduction. You also need to provide pointers to relevant background material that doesn’t make sense to include directly, so that novice readers can understand your results. You need to set your work in its proper context, especially in the introduction, by comparing it to existing work. In short, you should write the background section based on your own knowledge of the topic, which already relies on the work of others, but you should also make that reliance explicit.

Question: How prevalent is plagiarism among undergraduate students at American universities and colleges?
Answer: Roughly 20–30% of American undergraduates plagiarize at least once. Contrary to what another answer says, we actually have a lot of data about this, thanks largely to the research of Donald McCabe and his colleagues. The following table appears in this 2001 survey of over a decade of academic integrity research. Each column shows the percentage of surveyed students—each from multiple institutions—who admitted to having committed each type of academic misconduct at least once. The 1990–91 and 1995–96 studies separated responses from universities with honor codes and those without. Obviously there is no way to know how many students plagiarized but didn’t admit to plagiarism in the survey. More recent statistics are presumably available in this 2022 book by Rettinger and Gallant, but I don’t have access to a legal online copy (cough). But everyone should also be aware of the following “plea bargaining” study. Study participants were told that the study was about group versus individual problem solving. Pairs of students were put into rooms; each pair was given a sequence of logic problems to solve together, followed by another sequence of logic problems to solve individually. In each room, only one student was actually a subject; the other was part of the research team. In half of the rooms, during the individual-work phase, the researcher asked the subject cheating questions like “What did you get for problem 2?”. The (small!) number of students who ignored these questions were removed from the study. In the other half of the room, the researcher stayed quiet; none of the subjects asked cheating questions. After the second test phase, the subjects — whether innocent or guilty — were accused of cheating and offered a plea deal. If they admitted cheating, they would lose the reward for participating in the study, and that would end the matter; if they refused to admit cheating, they woudl be reported to the university’s Academic Review Board. Over half of the innocent students admitted to cheating.

Question: Is the fact that different human minds can develop similar ideas and concepts sufficient proof that these thoughts exist separately from the mind in a non-material reality?
Answer: No. It’s impossible to prove anything without first agreeing on the precise meaning of what you’re proving. What exactly is a “thought”? What exactly do you mean by “exist” and “separately”? What exactly is a “reality”, and what exactly does it mean for a reality to be “non-material”? Sure, we all have vague ideas about what these things mean, but proof requires precision. Maybe “different humans can think X” can serve as a useful definition of the phrase “X exists separately from the mind in a non-material reality”. Maybe. Personally, I find “different humans can think X” to be more useful phrasing; it’s shorter, it’s clearer, and it has less philosophical baggage. I’m perfectly content to consider “thoughts” nothing but patterns of electrical impulses in the brain. Thus, thoughts do not exist in a separate non-material reality; they exist in exactly the same material reality as cockroaches and lightning and hot-air balloons, as patterns of electrical impulses in brains. The fact that different people can have similar thoughts is evidence that (1) different human brains are similar, and (2) language works. If you mean something else by “thought”, you’re going to have to spell it out.

Question: How do you determine if an author has submitted the same manuscript to multiple journals?
Answer: The usual method is to ask highly qualified experts on the specific, narrow topic of the paper to referee that paper. For most research papers, the number of highly qualified experts is actually quite small—typically less than twenty, sometimes less than five. So if an author has submitted the same paper to multiple journals, and the editor of each submitted journal asks three of those experts for a referee report, there is a fair to good chance that the same expert will be asked for a referee report more than once. At least in the fields I work in, submitting the same paper to multiple journals at the same time is considered extremely unethical. Journal editors and referees (and in computer science, conference program committee members and reviewers) are unpaid volunteers, who offer their utterly necessary necessary services to benefit the research community, and to pay back people who reviewed their papers in the past. Their time and energy are limited resources. In the end, only one journal can accept and print the paper; parallel submissions complete waste all but one journal’s time and effort. If you submit the same paper to multiple journals and get caught, your paper is very likely to be desk-rejected from both journals, and those journals are likely to bar you from submitting again, at least for a few years. Just don’t.

Question: What was the topic of your master's thesis or doctoral dissertation?
Answer: I didn’t actually have a master’s thesis—I passed the PhD qualifying exam instead—but I did publish a paper that could have served as my thesis. My advisor and I developed fast algorithms for problems of the following form: Given a set P of n points in the plane, find the “smallest” subset of k points in P . Here “smallest” is defined by some geometric measure like diameter, or width, or radius of the smallest enclosing circle, or perimeter of the bounding box. There’s a slightly different algorithm for each measure, but they all follow roughly the same pattern. Using some data structure magic, we reduce the problem to about O ( n / k ) instances of finding the best k points out of a set of size O ( k ) . My PhD thesis was about the limits of efficient algorithms for a few simple geometric decision problems. For example, I proved that finding collinear triples in a given set of n points in the plane requires Ω ( n 2 ) time if you are only allowed to ask questions of the form “Is this triple of points oriented clockwise, oriented counterclockwise, or are the points collinear?” I also showed that, given n points and n lines in the plane, any “geometric divide-and-conquer algorithm” requires at least Ω ( n 4 / 3 ) time to decide whether any of the given points lies on any of the given lines. Both of these lower bounds match the running times of the fastest algorithms known at the time.

Question: How do we parse and get valid conclusions from the millions of scientific papers being published every year?
Answer: We don’t. Each of us pays attention to the tiny sliver of the scientific literature that is directly relevant to our own narrow expertise and interests. Even the most brilliant, curious, polymathic, expert researcher can reasonably expect to read and truly understand/absorb at most 10 papers a day. Crudely rounding up, let’s call that at most 5000 papers per year. That’s 0.1% of the roughly 5 million papers that were published in 2022. (This is a wildly generous upper bound. There are individual scientific papers that require even the most brilliant, curious, polymathic, expert researchers months or even years to fully understand/absorb.) Instead, we rely on other people—and communities of people—with interests and expertise different from our own to extract valid conclusions from their tiny slivers of the scientific literature.

Question: What average score out of 100 for all problem sets & exams will be good enough to get an A in all or most STEM courses at Caltech?

Perfect answers are usually worth 100%, and blank pages are usually worth 0%, but even those are not iron-clad rules.) instructors at US universities have wide latitude in setting grading standards. Even if the question could be answered, the answer would be useless. Suppose the correct answer were “92%”. What would that number actually tell you? Instructors also have wide latitude in calibrating the difficulty of their problem sets and exams. Just as importantly, different topics are difficult in different ways—some may require only memorization; others may require more analysis and synthesis; others may be judged primarily on clarity and precision; still others may judged primarily on the creativity of the submissions. If you want all As, be prepared to work your ass off. There is no such thing as “good enough”; there is only “better than yesterday”. This answer applies to arbitrary values of “Caltech”.

Name: Jeff Erickson
Question: What do you say about an optoelectronic engineering student that wants to tackle one of the unsolved mathematical problems? How hard is it? How many books must be read?
Answer: As a general rule I don’t recommend spending significant time trying to solve any of the big open question in mathematics until after (1) you get a mathematics PhD and (2) you get tenure. There’s nothing wrong with spending half an hour on the weekend puttering about with the Collatz conjecture or twin primes or P vs NP. Just remember two things. First, at least tens of thousands of incredibly smart, dedicated, and talented people—all with stronger math backgrounds than you—have been attacking these problems for decades. The complete literature on what little partial progress has been made would take most trained experts years to read and understand. Second, most big open problems of the past were not solved using elementary tricks, even when they were solved by “amateurs”. Not Fermat’s Last Theorem. Not the Kepler conjecture. Not the Poincaré conjecture. Not the Four-Color Theorem. Not linear programming in polynomial time. Not maximum matching in polynomial time. Not even prime detection in polynomial time. Of course there are exceptions (including, I think, David Smith’s recent discovery of aperiodic monotiles), but they are extremely rare. Evidence strongly suggests that making publishable progress on any famous open math problem requires deep mathematical knowledge, most of which doesn’t exist yet, in addition to insight, creativity, discipline, and a significant amount of luck. If you enjoy doing math for the sake of doing math, then by all means, enjoy yourself. But if your only motivation for doing math is becoming famous, you’re chasing a fantasy. Train for the race, not the trophy. (This advice works for abtrirary values of “doing math”.)

Question: A faculty told his/her grad students in his lab that their thoughts cannot override his thoughts. He/she asked them to leave the lab if they can’t follow this rule. What should students do?
Answer: Leave the lab. Run, don’t walk. A student’s thoughts can absolutely override a professor’s thoughts, if the experimental data is more consistent with the student’s thoughts than the professor’s. If the professor doesn’t recognize this basic scientific tenet, they are either scientifically or ethically unqualified to advise PhD students.

Name: Jeff Erickson
Question: What does this email of a potential PhD supervisor mean: "I hereby acknowledge receipt of your project. Thank you. I will get back to you next week."?
Answer: It means exactly what it says: If they had meant something else, they would have used different words. You cannot read minds. Don’t try. Trying to divine the hidden meaning in an email is a waste of your time and insulting to the email’s author.

Name: Jeff Erickson
Question: What are the best research topics on Corporate Social Responsibility?
Answer: The ones that you care about and are most informed about.

Name: Jeff Erickson
Question: How do I challenge myself with a new field of study? What are the most difficult or advanced fields of study which are less explored so far?
Answer: Focus on finding a field of study that genuinely interests you. In particular, look for a field that you enjoy being frustrated by, where you can be motivated by your own confusion and ignorance rather than discouraged.

Name: Jeff Erickson
Question: Why can't the powerful scientific community unite to surpass XD Dongfang and make greater breakthroughs, yet stifle and defame such a great discoverer, Mathematics & Nature ( https://www.mathnature.net/ )?
Answer: [A2A] The powerful scientific community has united to surpass XD Dongfang and make greater breakthroughs, by ignoring XD Dongfang and making breakthroughs. Mathematics & Nature is not a journal; it’s the personal blog of XD Dongfang. Journals have editorial boards with more than one person. Journals publish submissions by more than one person. Journals mostly publish papers by people who have no editing responsibilities. Journals subject their submissions to independent peer-review. By publishing Mathematics & Nature, and in particular by calling it a journal, and by persistently referring to himself as a “great discoverer” and his results as “breakthroughs”, XD Dongfang is labelling himself a crank. The powerful scientific community doesn’t need to stifle XD Dongfang; he’s doing a perfectly fine job of stifling himself.

Name: Jeff Erickson
Question: What’s the chance to get into one of the top US colleges to major in math/CS if I don’t have any international olympiad awards? I do have a bronze and a silver medal in my national math olympiad and I am a good student but not much else.
Answer: The vast majority of math and computer science majors at top US colleges don’t have any international olympiad awards. Not having an IMO award will not be a major detriment to your application. The number of awards given at the IMO is less than 300 per year, and most of the award winners do not attend US universities. Berkeley admits about 600 math and computer science majors per year. Now consider how many math and CS majors are admitted each year to Caltech, Chicago, CMU, Columbia, Cornell, Duke, Georgia Tech, Harvard, Harvey Mudd, Illinois, Johns Hopkins, Michigan, MIT, NYU, Penn, Princeton, Stanford, UCLA, UT Austin, Washington, Yale, and so on, and so on, and so on. (This list of “top US colleges” is not exhaustive!!) All that said, admission to every top CS program is extremely competitive, as is admission into any major at top private universities (MIT, Harvard, Chicago, etc.) Even having an IMO gold medal would not guarantee admission to math at Princeton or computer science at CMU, especially if “good student” isn’t a humble synonym for “stellar student”. Of course you should apply, but remember that each application is a lottery ticket.

Name: Jeff Erickson
Question: What are the necessary conditions and requirements of getting into a master in CS, IS, or AI at UCLA or UIUC from UNC Pembroke as an international student (three years in my home country and senior year at UNC Pembroke, receiving degrees from both)?
Answer: The official admissions requirements are listed on the web pages of each graduate program. The actual de facto admissions requirements are significantly more stringent; the number of applicants that satisfy the minimal requirements far exceeds the number of students we can admit. The computer science department at Illinois offers two master’s degrees. The School of Information Sciences also offers a master’s degree in information management. Since this is outside my department, I’m less familiar with the de facto application requirements and admission rates.

Name: Jeff Erickson
Question: What is the possibility of applying for UCLA or UIUC from Pembroke, NC? What are the conditions?
Answer: Your chances of being admitted to Illinois are anywhere from slightly lower to significantly lower than an Illinois resident with a similar application, depending on your intended major/college. Like every other public state university, UIUC has a mandate to educate students in its own state, so out-of-state (and international) students are held to higher admission standards. I assume the same is true of UCLA. You can find the profiles of typical first-year students in various colleges at Illinois on the university web site. (Again, these are profiles for all first-year students; out of state students tend to be stronger on average.) But unless you’re aiming for a program that just doesn’t exist in North Carolina, you’re probably better off applying to UNC Chapel Hill or NC State.

Name: Jeff Erickson
Question: It is my opinion that if an academic paper is submitted for publication and not a single error can be pointed out within it, that it should be published irrelevant of whether the conclusion is unpopular, am I wrong?
Answer: [A2A] I don’t know why you’ve asked for my opinion after getting so many consistent answers over the last three years, but here goes. Yes, you are wrong. The other answers explain why you are wrong. I am absolutely not a physics expert, but to my untrained eyes your result looks like the equivalent of proving the cows aren’t spherical. A model that assumes a point mass at the end of a massless, frictionless string with infinite tensile strength (in a vacuum, in an inertial reference frame, etc.) doesn’t accurately predict the behavior of a real ball spinning at the end of a real string? Quelle surprise!! Instead of concluding that physics is garbage, I’d recommend trying to understand precisely where the assumptions of your model break down, in particular by actually experimenting with real balls at the end of real string (instead of just relying on “common sense”), and/or by asking experts for help (instead of assuming a priori that experts are wrong). There is something significant here that you don’t understand. That’s awesome! What an incredible opportunity to learn!

Name: Jeff Erickson
Question: Have you ever seen a student's willingness to sacrifice/jeopardize high grades/GPA (e.g., taking harder classes outside their "comfort zone"; unusual research projects/extra-curriculars) pay off intellectually, academically, or in career trajectory?
Answer: YES. In fact, I think this description applies to a significant majority of successful people that I’ve met during my 30-something years in academia. (Admittedly, it’s not always easy to tell. A small minority of super-strong students take significant risks, taking harder classes well outside their comfort zone, and still manage to get nothing but As.) I have also seen plenty of 4.0-GPA students completely flounder outside the narrow confines of academia, where all problems have relatively short, relatively simple, well-structured solutions that only use techniques that can be taught in a single term, and that an expert can solve in at most a few days. This isn’t just my personal opinion. My (top-5 US computer science) department’s PhD program rejects a significant majority of applicants with perfect undergraduate grades, even when they come from stellar departments like MIT, Berkeley, Stanford, or CMU. We’d much rather admit a student with a 3.0 GPA and a strong research portfolio than a student with a 4.0 GPA who has done nothing else.

Name: Jeff Erickson
Question: What is your review of the Journal of Geocentric cosmology?
Answer: [A2A] Journal of Geocentric Cosmology appears to be the personal blog of one Dr. Steven Alonzo, who is simultaneously its founder, its only editor, and (as far as I can tell) its only published author. It has published no papers, only a series of “posts” by Dr. Alonzo. The “journal” site includes a link to Flat Earth University, founded in 2023 by one Dr. Steven Alonzo, who is the only human being mentioned on the university web site. The URL of the FEU’s web site ends with “.university”, not “.edu”. FEU claims to have campuses in New York City, Toronto, and San Pedro, Belize, and it waxes poetic about about life in Belize, but it doesn’t advertise the precise location of any of these campuses, which strongly suggests that they don’t exist. The FEU web site lists exactly one class, which I was able to complete in about five minutes, and which apparently grants me a bachelor’s degree (see below). Elsewhere on the site, FEU claims to offer both bachelor’s and master’s degrees in Geocentric Cosmology, which take 3 years and 5 years respectively. Somehow, “year after year”, the master’s program “attracts the brightest minds from around the world”, despite being at most one year old and not necessarily existing. An admissions information page suggests that one can apply for admission by filling out an online application form, but I was unable to find an online application form on the web site. So if this is a scam, it’s a weirdly ineffective scam. The web sites of both the Journal of Geocentric Cosmology and Flat Earth University are quite polished, much more so than most scam university or vanity journal sites. I have to wonder if these aren’t elaborate background props for an alternate-universe-academia fanfic series or live-action role-playing game. tl;dr: I recommend reading Connie Willis, Neal Stephenson, or Terry Pratchett instead.

Name: Jeff Erickson
Question: Suppose an academic journal already exists for the topic you want to publish on while that journal refuses to publish your manuscript. Why could you start a new journal on the same topic?
Answer: Unless you are already well-established in your field, and you can convince a dozen or two equally well-established experts in your field to serve as your editorial board, any journal you start would be completely ignored by the research community you are trying to reach with your paper. Why should we trust that the papers in your journal underwent stringent peer-review? Why should we trust the decisions of your journal’s editorial board? And what is this? The first paper in the journal was written by the journal’s editor-in-chief? Even with an expert editorial board, that’s the kiss of death. If you want your journal to be taken seriously, you also need to convince a few dozen well-established experts in your field, preferably excluding everyone on your editorial board, to submit strong papers to the first several issues of your journal. And even you successfully found a journal that the research community trusts, you are now saddled with the burden of maintaining the journal—tracking submissions, making desk-reject decisions, identifying referees, identifying new editors, maintaining the journal web site, negotiating with journal indexers—for years, if not decades. This way lies madness. No, the correct course of action is to revise your paper to address the concerns raised by the referees for the first journal—Yes, even referee #2—and then submit the revised paper to a different journal. (There is no such thing as a paper that is only in scope for a single journal.)

Name: Jeff Erickson
Question: I have 3.88 UW, 4.64 W, and 1300 SAT. Can I get into a UIUC mathematics major?
Answer: Mmmaybe. To be a math major at Illinois, you would apply for admission to the College of Liberals Arts and Sciences (LAS) Your unweighted GPA is close to the median for first-year LAS students, but your SAT score is well below the 25th percentile. So I would guess that you have a decent chance. Your chances are higher if you already live in Illinois, and higher still if you write a compelling application essay. Illinois is test-optional—you don’t have to submit your SAT or ACT scores with your application—but I don’t know what effect omitting your test scores would actually have in practice. But I would also strongly recommend applying to at least a few other universities; don’t plan on being accepted to Illinois.

Name: Jeff Erickson
Question: Can an undergraduate be allowed to audit post-graduate courses (PhD)?
Answer: Sure. Just ask the instructor for permission to sit in on their lectures. If they say yes, you’re in—no need to fill out the formal audit paperwork. (And if they say no, you’re out—no formal audit paperwork will help you.) In fact, undergrads can even take post-graduate courses for credit. I’ve taught about 20 graduate-level courses; every single one of them included at least three undergraduates, and the undergrads usually performed in the top half of the class. In my department, undergrads who want to take a grad-level course for credit just need to fill out a form that asks for the instructor’s permission. Obviously, different instructors, departments, and universities have different policies. I suggest starting by asking the instructor.

Name: Jeff Erickson
Question: I started working on a systematic review paper and my research topic has changed halfway through, my supervisor still wants to me finish the paper that will not be used for my research, should I complete or challenge him?
Answer: I have two objections. First, the purpose of writing papers isn’t to help your own research; it’s to help other people’s research. Second, the skills you develop by writing a systematic review paper will be useful for your research, even if the review paper itself is not. You might consider having a discussion (not a “challenge”) with your advisor about whether the time you are spending developing long-term research skills by finishing the review paper might be better spent on short-term research goals more directly related to your thesis. Research requires all sort of strategic choices—for example, whether to focus on short-term versus long-term goals—between options that are sometimes at conflict. Part of your advisor’s job is to help you learn to navigate those choices, so it’s perfectly appropriate to ask them why they want you to finish the review paper, and how they expect that effort to impact progress toward your degree.

Name: Jeff Erickson
Question: Which is most promising, financially and other wise, for an undergraduate to consider for masters study; biology or life science, environmental science, nutrition, public health, business administration, data science or analytics, education?
Answer: Wow. You’re all over the place. I think you’re going about this completely backward. Your first question should be “What career do I want?” followed by “What exactly do I need to obtain that career?” If the answer to the second question includes a masters degree, it will include a master’s degree in a particular field. A master’s degree degree itself is utterly worthless, except to pass some stupid HR checklist; what matters are the skills that the degree helps you develop. Said differently: The master’s degree field that is the most promising for you is the one that best matches your interests, your experience, and your career goals. If nothing else, you’ll perform better in a degree program that you’re prepared for and that you actually care about. So: First choose a career path. Pick something (1) that you’re likely to be good at, (2) that you’re likely to find rewarding, (3) that other people are likely to pay you to do, and (4) that lets you solve more problems than you create. Then ask whether that career path includes a master’s degree.

Name: Jeff Erickson
Question: What is the lowest impact factor for a scientific journal that you have ever seen?
Answer: Zero. I have seen journals being launched. By definition, immediately after a journal publishes its first issue, it has an impact factor of zero, because nobody has published a paper that cites a paper in that journal.

Name: Jeff Erickson
Question: How can I publish a research paper on my own without my professor's help? Which journal should I choose as a communication major?
Answer: How can I publish a research paper on my own without my professor's help? Choose a journal to submit to. (See below.) Follow the submission instructions on the journal’s web site, and follow them precisely. Wait for the referee reports. If your paper is rejected, revise it to address any concerns raised in the referee reports and resubmit it to a different journal (restarting the process). If your paper is not rejected, revise it as directed by the editor, in response to concerns raised in the referee reports. Curse Referee #2. Repeat until the editor accepts the paper. Read the galley proofs extremely carefully, because the copy editor will introduce significant errors. Submit the corrected galley proofs. Sign the copyright transfer form / publication agreement. Wait for the paper to appear on the publisher’s web site. In other words, exactly the same way as your advisor (and everyone else) would do it. Which journal should I choose as a communication major? That obviously depends on the content and intended audience of your paper, but as a general rule of thumb, I recommend submitting to the journal that your paper cites the most.

Name: Jeff Erickson
Question: Is there any website where I can publish my research paper for free (even if it's just online publication) and can give me a professional or official certification of publication?
Answer: I’ve never paid to publish anything, so… Any relevant journal or conference? Of course, the paper has to survive peer review (which takes anywhere from a few weeks to several months) before it is actually published. At least in computer science, legitimate venues do not charge authors to publish; in particular, legitimate open-access venues do not charge authors to publish open-access papers. Another possibility is arXiv or a similar preprint server. Papers on arXiv aren’t peer-reviewed (which misleads some people into thinking they’re not “published”), and they appear within 24 hours of submission. However, you do need to find a published researcher in your field to sponsor you if you haven’t posted on arXiv before. Whether the publication is “just online” or also on paper is utterly immaterial. To first approximation, nobody reads paper any more. Many long-standing journals still produce paper copies—mostly archival copies for libraries—but online-only journals are increasingly common. I don’t know what “a professional or official certification of publication” is. Most publication venues (including arXiv) indicate when the paper was submitted. The fact that the paper appears on the venue’s web site is concrete evidence that the paper is published, because “appears on the venue’s website” is the definition of “published by the venue”.

Name: Jeff Erickson
Question: My professors encourage their students to dig deep into the course content, yet whenever I ask a question they say, "That is beyond the scope of this class". Any advice on how to ask better questions?
Answer: Let me start by echoing what other people have already written: Unless you are asking specifically about the content of today’s lecture, the right time to ask your questions is either after class or in office hours, not during the lecture itself. The point of lectures is to communicate information that the entire class needs to know, to the entire class. If answering your question doesn’t help a significant fraction of the students, it’s not a good question to ask in lecture. Even in office hours, learn to read the room. If there are a bunch of people waiting to ask questions about this week’s course material — and in particular, this week’s homework or upcoming exam — they have priority. (Unless the instructor says otherwise, of course.) Even in office hours, sometimes “beyond the scope of the class” means “I don’t have the three weeks / six months / five years that it would require to answer your question (or worse, to explain why your question doesn’t make any sense). It’s complicated and hard, and you are not ready.” Digging deep into the course material means digging deep into the course material, not material that would take one or two or six more courses to explain, and certainly not about potential applications of the course material to post-quantum artificial general intelligence. Even in office hours, sometimes “beyond the scope of the class” means “I think you’re asking that question to show off how smart you are. Just stop. Nobody cares how smart you are. If you really want to impress me, master the course material.” Remember that you are still learning. In particular, you are still learning to match your intuition with the course material. So of course you’re going to have questions, based on your intuition, that are out of scope. The response “That’s out of scope for the class” tells you that your intuition is leading you astray, at least for the moment, and you’d be better off concentrating on the results and techniques developed in class. Good intuition is the result of practice and experience, not a substitute for it.

Name: Jeff Erickson
Question: What are the other top 3 STEM schools in the world besides Caltech & MIT? Are LAC or STEM colleges or universities more popular with the top students? Why?
Answer: What are the other top 3 STEM schools in the world besides Caltech & MIT? The question is based on the false premise that there is such a thing as “the top 5 STEM schools”. Different schools are better or worse for different ((sub)sub)fields, for different metrics, and for different students. In particular, Caltech and MIT are very different from each other and from most other universities, and while most of the students at those two universities thrive, there are myriads of brilliant STEM students for whom Caltech and MIT would be utter torture. For those students, Caltech and MIT are the worst STEM schools. Are LAC or STEM colleges or universities more popular with the top students? Why? This question is based on the false premise that there is a universal ground-truth definition of “top students”. There are excellent students—brilliant, passionate, successful, happy students with rewarding and lucrative careers in their future—at every liberal arts college, at every STEM college, and at every university. Arguing about whether MIT or Caltech or Reed or Harvard or ETHZ or Tsinghua or Bucksnort Community College has the most smartest bestest shiniest gloriousest students is pointless. Utterly and completely pointless. If you want good mathematicians, look at their math. If you want good chemists, look at their chemistry. If you want good gardeners, look at their gardens. If you want good trout farmers, taste their trout.

Name: Jeff Erickson
Question: How much time will I need to learn data structures and algorithms if I am an amateur?
Answer: As much time as you’re willing to spend. I’ve been learning algorithms and data structures for at least 40 years, and I’m still not done.

Name: Jeff Erickson
Question: What could make a PhD advisor not willing to let go of a PhD student despite bad treatment by the advisor?
Answer: Oh, that’s easy. Bullies likes to keep their victims close. On the other hand, it really doesn’t matter whether the advisor is “willing to let go” of a PhD student. If a student wants to leave, they can just leave.

Name: Jeff Erickson
Question: What happens to the grades given out in graduate level math courses at colleges or universities? Do all graduate students always get an A or some of them can get B or C or D or F?
Answer: What happens to the grades given out in graduate level math courses at colleges or universities? They go into the students’ transcripts, just like undergraduate grades, where (unless they fall below some required minimum) they are mostly ignored. Do all graduate students always get an A or some of them can get B or C or D or F? No, graduate students do not always get A’s. It’s fair to guess that A is by far the most common grade, but lower grades are definitely possible. For example, graduate students who register for a class and then don’t participate (don’t submit homework, don’t sit exams, don’t submit required projects, etc.) are given Fs. In my advanced algorithms course, typically about half of the graduate students earn As, about half earn B’s, and less than 5% earn C’s or below. As a more nuanced example: The math department at Illinois requires all PhD students to receive credit for five graduate-level “comprehensive” courses (chosen from a longer list). A student can receive credit for a “comp course” either taking the course and receiving a B+ or better, or by taking a special examination. The comp courses are intentionally famously hard; a significant fraction of the students score below a B+ and have to take the exam the following semester. Failing a comp class outright (which is rare but does happen) is taken as a sign that the student is just not prepared for the PhD program.

Name: Jeff Erickson
Question: What is most considered for getting a full ride scholarship for an international undergraduate student with 2 gap year and have no international award?
Answer: By far the most common full-ride scholarship for American university students—and with extremely rare exceptions, the only full-ride scholarship available to international students—is the Parents-Pay-For-Everything Scholarship. The most significant selection criterion for the PPFE Scholarship is whether your parents can afford to pay for everything. tl,dr: It’s not going to happen.

Name: Jeff Erickson
Question: Are there prestigious universities that allow computer science faculty members to work remotely 100% of the time, even if they reside in a different location in the world?
Answer: Yes, but extremely rarely. I have a couple of colleagues that have held faculty appointments at multiple universities in different countries. These dual positions allow them, for example, to spend the regular academic year teaching in one country, and then spend their summers doing research in another country. But these are both extraordinary exceptions. (Some people might argue that Bojan and János aren’t computer scientists, but I think that’s hair-splitting.) Two other mechanisms for working at a university while living somewhere else are sabbaticals / leaves of absence and changing institutions. Sabbaticals allow faculty to work at another institution, typically for a year, while maintaining their faculty positions and even drawing a partial salary. Faculty can take leaves of absence that last multiple years, almost always without pay, to develop startup companies. Finally, it’s common for faculty moving from one university to another to maintain at least an adjunct position at their old school for a year or more, until their old-school PhD students finish their degrees. But again, these are exceptions. Most universities allow only a small fraction of their faculty to be on sabbatical/leave at the same time, and moves from one university to another are relatively rare. Almost all universities require their faculty to spent almost all of their time on campus. After all, by default, all university faculty are expected to teach, advise/mentor students, and serve on university committees, all of which are best done in person. tl;dr: For all practical purposes, no.

Name: Jeff Erickson
Question: If you conduct any published research, do you publish it through open access?
Answer: Yes, whenever possible. In particular, I regularly post versions of my papers (1) to my own personal web site and (2) to arXiv. So even if the official publication venue is not open-access, there are open-access versions of the paper available. I’ve published about 100 papers over the last 30 years; not one publisher has ever objected (or, I suspect, even noticed). I have never paid to have a paper published open-access. But over time, more and more conferences and journals are switching to either diamond open access or limited-time paywalls, so it’s usually easy to steer away from venues whose publishers use permanent locks. There are exceptions—papers that are clearly best suited for one particular conference, which happens to use a closed-access publisher. But that’s why the gods gave us arXiv.

Name: Jeff Erickson
Question: Why can't Caltech & MIT offer any math courses that are similar in content & rigor as Math 55 at Harvard? Isn't against the copyright and/or patent rules of Harvard?
Answer: They can. But why would they? They offer their own math classes that they believe serve their students better.

Name: Jeff Erickson
Question: I have a 3.7GPA and 1480 SAT can I get into any good universities (ideally for CS or engineering) with average extracuriculars?
Answer: Probably, yes. I have to disagree with David Miller’s answer. He’s using campus-wide statistics for UIUC, but almost all engineering majors (and all engineering CS majors) declare their major when they apply, and some majors (like CS) are significantly more competitive than others. Your GPA is below the middle 50% for the Fall 2023 incoming class of engineering students at Illinois, and your SAT score is near to bottom of the middle 50%. So I think you’d have a fair chance of being admitted into most engineering majors at Illinois, but more competitive majors like mechanical engineering would be more of a stretch, and computer science is probably out of reach. These acceptance rates are a little deceptive; there is a lot of self-selection. For example, the out-of-state acceptance rate for electrical engineering was 55% in 2022, but the average SAT score among accepted EE students that year was 1517. On the other hand, your SAT scores are either close to or above the 75th percentile of new engineering students at Maryland[1], Minnesota[2], NC State[3], and Ohio State,[4]all of which are ranked among the top 25 undergraduate engineering programs in the country by US News.[5] Unofficial sources suggest your profile might also be competitive at Colorado, Texas A&M, Penn State, Virginia Tech, and Wisconsin. (Most universities I looked into don’t advertise 25–75% ranges for engineering students; in fact, most don’t advertise any data about first-year students.) These are (deliberately) all state universities, so your admission chances are higher if you are a resident of their state. And computer science is more competitive everywhere than other engineering majors.

Name: Jeff Erickson
Question: How would/does academia handle research that is done by people with no qualifications? Assuming the research passes/could pass peer review etc.
Answer: Nobody ever asks for your diploma when you submit a paper. Certain types of research—specifically, research with animal or human subjects—require ethical oversight that is typically only available to tenure-track faculty at universities and to senior research staff at hospitals, research centers, and the like. You cannot publish a clinical trial for a cancer drug unless you have a doctorate, because you can’t get the job required to ask for the ethical clearance to perform the trial unless you have a doctorate, and you can’t publish human-subjects research that hasn’t been cleared by an ethics board. Similarly, it is nearly impossible to obtain access to certain laboratory equipment (reagents, particle accelerators, FMRI machines, virus samples, …) without a job that requires a doctorate. But if you want to do research in theoretical physics, or mathematics, or computer science, or field biology, or economics, or astronomy, or electrical engineering, or any number of other fields, absolutely nothing is stopping you. The only barrier to entry for publishing research in those fields is producing good research; it is utterly irrelevant whether the author is a tenured full professor or a retired janitor. And then academia handles it just like any other good research—as good research! People cite papers, not diplomas.

Name: Jeff Erickson
Question: If you publish your own paper then get recognised for the science after college, would the first paper be recognised? You haven't started a PhD or even college but have conducted research. Will it be as if you made the discovery now or the future?
Answer: If you publish a peer-reviewed scientific research paper, you have been recognized for the research in the paper. That’s what publishing a peer-reviewed paper means. Whether you graduate from college twenty years before or twenty years after publishing is utterly immaterial. For example, when he was still a high school student, John Pardon proved a powerful generalization of the Carpenter’s Rule Theorem to arbitrary simple rectifiable closed curves. (“Simple” means that the curve doesn’t intersect itself; “rectifiable” means (crudely) it has finite length.) Pardon proved that it is possible to continuously deform any simple rectifiable closed curve in the plane into a convex curve, keeping the length of the curve fixed, without ever decreasing the distance between two points on the curve. Intuitively, we can blow up any two-dimensional balloon. It took a couple of years to review, as is common for math journal papers, so Pardon was a college student when his result was actually published. Nevertheless, he is given credit for proving his theorem as a high school student, because that’s when he actually did it.

Name: Jeff Erickson
Question: What are research proposals on diplomacy and governance in a master’s thesis?
Answer: A research proposal is just what it says on the tin—a proposal to perform some research. A good research proposal describes a small number of specific research questions, surveys the relevant literature (to convince the reader that these research questions are both open and interesting), and describes a specific and realistic plan to carry out the research (to convince the reader that answering those research questions in a short period of time is realistic). But before you can start writing a research proposal, you need find good research questions. That requires reading a significant chunk of the relevant literature, looking for gaps in the world’s knowledge. You need to understand what’s known about a topic before you can start exploring the unknown. You need to understand what questions your audience (and yes, everything you write has an audience) will find interesting before you can propose an interesting question. You need to understand standard research results and processes and techniques in your field before you can develop a realistic research plan. In short, first you need to read. A LOT. Your advisor can help you by suggesting specific topics to read about, or specific publication venues to explore, or specific authors to read from. From there you can chase references backward, chase citations forward, and explore other works by the same authors, or in the same values, or with the same keywords in the title. After a week or so, report back to your advisor what you’ve read and discuss next steps. Repeat five or six times. Once you settle on a topic, you can start thinking about research questions and how you might answer them. Your advisor can help you winnow out your bad ideas. And you will have bad ideas, because everybody has bad ideas. Most ideas are bad. Once you have questions and a realistic path to answer them, you can start writing. Once you’ve written everything, then you have a research proposal! Congratulations! Expect this process to take months.

Question: How do I raise my GPA from a 3.42 to 3.7-3.8 in a span of one school year? What grades are needed?

That’s just barely in the range you specified. If you’re already finished more than one year, then raising your GPA to 3.8 in one year is mathematically impossible.

Name: Jeff Erickson
Question: Considering dropping out of Ph.D even though advisor wants me to graduate soon. How can I broach this to him without burning any bridges? No publications and no meaningful skills gained from the program at all sadly.
Answer: [A2A] As others have pointed out, something is badly out of whack here. Either your advisor is badly overestimating your progress, or you are badly underestimating your progress. Either way, you should have a serious face-to-face talk with your advisor about your concerns. And you need to have it now, before you make any decisions about dropping out. Ask your advisor directly, to their face, in so many words, what you need to do to complete your PhD, and whether they believe that you have the necessary skills and experience and momentum finish soon. Note well: Not whether your advisor believes you should have those skills, but whether they believe you actually do have those skills. Tell your advisor directly, to their face, in so many words, that you are concerned about your lack of publications. Tell your advisor directly, to their face, in so many words, that you don’t feel that you have gained any meaningful skills. Tell your advisor directly, in so many words, that because of your apparent lack of progress, you are not convinced that completing your PhD is a realistic goal. Don’t worry about “burning bridges”. If your advisor responds with anger or impatience (not just disappointment), or simply refuses to have the discussion, you have your answer—don’t walk, run. This is not someone you want as an advisor or even as a reference. Let the bridge burn. But ideally, your advisor will remind you that almost every researcher goes through periods of self-doubt, feeling like they’ve made no progress in years, wondering if they’ll be able to reach their next goal. Sometimes that goal is a PhD; sometimes it’s a faculty job; sometimes is a research grant; sometimes it’s tenure; and sometimes it’s all of the above. (Hi.) And then you and your advisor can have an honest discussion about what you’ve actually done. Ideally, nothing that comes up in that discussion will surprise your advisor. Ideally, you’ve been meeting regularly with your advisor since you started withing with them, and you’ve been open with them about what you’ve done since the last meeting, and they’ve been open with you about their expectations for the next meeting.milestone. After all, that’s their job as an advisor (and part of your job as a PhD student). But I have a feeling that communication has been less than ideal so far. The best time to fix that is now. The discussion could go any number of directions: None of these is burning bridges. Some of these options might be scarier than others. You may still want to quit even if your advisor convinces you that you could finish quickly, and that is totally your right, You might be devastated to learn that you’ll have to drop out, even though you were thinking of dropping out anyway. The discussion itself is likely to be emotionally exhausting, no matter what its outcome. Make sure you have a good emotional support network in place — friends and family at a minimum, professional counseling if possible.

Question: Why? It's award day at school. I studied hard but I did not win any medals. I get good grades so I thought I was a great student. I feel discouraged and stupid. My state exams are soon, but I don't think I'm good enough anymore.
Answer: Here you go: 🥇🌟🏆 Not worth much, is it? You already know that you are a great student, because you have the data to prove it. Trust the data, and trust yourself. You do not need to be the best student in the world to be a great student. Even if those trophies went to better students, the existence of better students does not negate the fact that you are a great student. And we have no way of knowing whether those awards actually went to better students; maybe they were chosen according to other criteria (for example: randomly from a set of equally good students), or maybe the judges were just incompetent. It’s not like their opinion actually matters. You can be a great pop singer without being Taylor Swift. You can be a great skateboarder without being Tony Hawk. You can be a great actor without winning an Oscar. You can be a great mathematician without winning a Fields Medal. You can be a great student without an award. Of course it’s nice to be recognized, but recognition doesn’t make you great. Greatness only means that you’re more likely to be recognized, and recognition only means that you’re more likely to be great. You know that you are a great student, no matter what anybody else thinks. Trust yourself.

My department doesn’t have a data structures and algorithms course. Name: Jeff Erickson
Question: What is your opinion regarding one going directly from undergraduate CS to master’s? Is it preferred by schools like CMU and Stanford that one have some work experience first?
Answer: What is your opinion regarding one going directly from undergraduate CS to master’s? Honestly, when I read the first sentence of your question, my first thought was “As opposed to what?!” I think most master’s students, at least in my department, apply directly as undergraduates. But that’s just a hypothesis. Let’s see if the actual data supports it! My department has two on-campus master’s degree programs: a research-based “Master of Science” (MS) and a terminal course-based “Master of Computer Science” (MCS). For each of these programs, we received about 2700 applications for Fall 2024 admission. Here are Fall 2024 acceptance numbers for the MS program, broken out by the year of the applicant’s undergraduate degree. The largest number of applications, the largest number of acceptances, and the largest fraction of acceptances are all from 2024; those applicants were all undergraduates when they applied. And here is the corresponding data for the (on-campus) MCS program. Again, the largest number of applications, the largest number of acceptances, and the largest acceptance rate were all for current undergraduates expecting to get their bachelor’s degrees in 2024. Applying in the first year after graduation is almost as good, but applying more than one year later seems to hurt significantly. tl;dr: Actual admission data supports the hypothesis that work experience is not a significant advantage, and may be a significant disadvantage, in applying to master’s programs at top CS programs in the US. In hindsight, this shouldn’t be too surprising. Admissions decisions are largely based on evidence that the applicant is prepared for graduate-level coursework and (for MS applicants) research. As a rule, graduate-level classes assume a strong undergraduate academic background. Research also requires a song academic background. The more time you spend away from school, the spongier your academic skills get. The skills that people develop with work experience are valuable and important for success in the professional world, but for most people, they are different. All that said, remember that every department makes its own graduate admissions decisions using its own criteria. If you really want to learn what a department looks for in its master’s-degree applicants, the best way to find out is to call the department’s graduate admissions office and ask them.
