Name: Jeff Erickson
Question: How can I find and get full scholarship for studying at UIUC as an international student? Thank you
Answer: (I’m going to assume that you’re talking about attending Illinois as an undergraduate, because graduate students have “assistantships” and “fellowships” much more often than “scholarships”.) If you are an absolutely amazing student—like the best in your country in five years—and you write a compelling application essay, then maybe you have a chance. Maybe. A small chance. tl;dr: To first approximation, you don’t. Let’s start at the financial aid office: Here’s the important sentence: For international students, financial aid is generally limited to institutional aid programs provided by the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign and outside scholarships obtained by you through private sources. “Institutional aid programs” means scholarships awarded by individual colleges or departments. With a few exceptions, you don’t need to do anything special to apply for these scholarships; applicants are automatically considered for all scholarships for which they are eligible when they apply. Actually winning such a scholarship is a different matter. Let’s look at the database of all scholarships: This is a list of all scholarships, not just scholarships available to incoming international students. If you select (for example) the College of Engineering from the drop-down menu, you’ll see a list of dozens of scholarships available to engineering students. Some of these are awarded only to juniors and seniors, and/or students in specific majors; others are only available to US residents, Illinois residents, or even applicants from more specific locations; some consider financial need; others are purely merit-based. Again, there’s nothing special that you need to do to apply to these; if you are eligible, you are automatically considered when you apply. That also means that there is absolutely no point in worrying about whether or not you’re going to get one. The College of Engineering also has a page describing its scholarships: Again, there is one important sentence: Awarding scholarships is based on a complete review of your application In other words, the best way to qualify for a scholarship is to have a compelling application—especially the application essay—that meets the criteria for that scholarship. Trying to game the system is pointless and self-defeating; there are too many different criteria. Your best bet is to put your best foot forward. Write an honest and compelling application essay about your interests, your experiences, your goals, your failures and successes. It’s also important to remember that different scholarships give different amounts of money. A few pay full tuition and housing costs; most pay only a few thousand. And naturally, scholarships that give larger amounts of money are given to fewer students. Most scholarships that cover tuition are awarded to at most one student (note well: not “at most one international student”) per year. The number of students whose tuition is completely covered by those dozens of Engineering scholarships is signficantly less than 100, and probably less than 10. There are more than 1500 international engineering undergraduates at Illinois. You do the math. International students are a significant source of income for the University of Illinois. For many years, the university has deliberately increased the number of international students it admits, at least partly in response to unfriendly state governments repeatedly and drastically cutting state contributions to higher education, or simply not giving universities the money supposedly allocated in the budget (cough cough). Those cuts to higher education are partly political, but the main motivation is the Illinois state legislature’s decade’s-long habit of delegating its constitutionally protected pension obligations to Future Legislatures. (For most of the last century, any elected state official—Democrat or Republican—who dared to utter the words “raise” and “taxes” in that order has been immediately voted out.) At this point, the University of Illinois could not operate without the tuition that international students bring in. It is simply not in the university’s interest to offer financial aid to a significant fraction of its international students. Finally, even if you had a full scholarship, you would still need enough money in the bank to support yourself for a year—including tuition, housing, and travel—to obtain a US student visa.

Question: How intelligent is artificial intelligence? Do I have to plug it in for it to work or does it power itself from within itself like naturally-occurring biologically rendered forms of universal electromagnetism? Are there quantum entanglements?
Answer: How intelligent is artificial intelligence? It’s not. It’s mostly fiction. Do I have to plug it in for it to work I assume you’re referring to the computers that so-called AI software runs on. (Do you need to feed English for it to work? No, English is not the kind of thing that can be fed. You don’t need to feed English books, but you do need to feed English speakers and English writers and English readers.) Whether you need to “plug it in” depends on the device. Many computers run on batteries. You might need to plug them in when the battery charge gets low, or you might need to attach them to another source of energy (like a running gasoline engine), or you might need to replace the old batteries with new ones. But every modern computer does require electricity. or does it power itself from within itself No. The second law of thermodynamics prevents that, for the same reason that it prevents perpetual motion. Batteries only work until they run out of charge, and every battery will eventually run out of charge. like naturally-occurring biologically rendered forms of universal electromagnetism? Wow. That is an impressive word salad. You should consider getting more sleep. Living things do not “power themselves from within themselves.” Living things need to get energy from the outside world, or they die. Plants get energy from the sun. Animals get energy by eating plants and other animals. Anyone using the phrase “universal electromagnetism” seriously is either deeply misinformed or is trying to scam you. Or both. Are there quantum entanglements? Yes, quantum entanglement exists, but it has absolutely nothing to do with AI. You might as well ask if there is gravity.

Question: What are the requirements of transferring to a computer science major in UC Berkeley from UC Davis?
Answer: This is a great question for Google. [Yells offstage] Hey, Google! “UC berkeley cs transfer requirements”! [Waits one second, gets results] Thanks, Google! The third link in my Google results seems the most useful: Here are the important bits: Transfer applicants must apply with 60–80 semester units completed by the end of the spring prior to fall matriculation. Students with too many “upper division” (junior and senior level) units are ineligible. The main criteria for admission to the College of Engineering is: Courses that cover or partially cover material in our department’s lower division courses required for graduation (but not admission) are strongly recommended; the more of these courses completed, the stronger the application will be. Therefore, when possible, it is to the applicant’s benefit to take courses in data structures, discrete math, probability, circuits, data structures, and C++ or Java. The link at the bottom of the EECS web page also seems useful: What are my chances of being admitted? The answer depends on the quality of the applicant pool and the number of spaces available in the major. For fall 2022, the College of Engineering admitted 336 transfer students (13.6% of applicants), who had an average GPA of 3.86. Keeping in mind that EECS is the most impacted major at Berkeley by a significant margin, I would expect the acceptance rate for EECS transfer applicants to be significantly lower than 13.6%, probably closer to 2–3%. But honestly, I strongly recommend not bothering. If you can succeed at Davis, there is no reason for you to transfer. If you can’t succeed at Davis, you won’t succeed at Berkeley either. tl;dr: Take enough core preparation and lower-division CS courses (but not too many!), get As in all of them, write a compelling statement describing why you cannot meet your academic goals at Davis, sacrifice a laptop to the ghost of Alan Turing, and plan to be rejected anyway.

Name: Jeff Erickson
Question: How come when you get 100 percent your grade barely goes up but if you get a 60 it drops so far?
Answer: Because your past grades have been in the 90s. A score that is close to the average of your previous scores doesn’t change your average score as much as a score that is far from the average of your previous scores. For example, suppose your class has five assignments, and you got a score of 90 on each of the first four assignments. So your average score before the last assignment is (drum roll) 90. This is just how averages work.

Name: Jeff Erickson
Question: What is the review of Purdue University Indy campus for engineering? Is it going to be more similar to Purdue University West Lafayette or more IUPUI?
Answer: [Someone who actually works at Purdue should sanity-check this answer; I’m writing from one state over.] Nobody knows yet. IUPUI formally ceases to exist on July 1, 2024. The programs at IUPUI that are administered by the Purdue system, including all engineering programs, are being rebranded as Purdue University in Indianapolis; programs administered by the Indiana University system are being rebranded as Indiana University Indianapolis. PUI advertises that it will offer exactly the same programs, with exactly the same classes and learning goals, as the Purdue West Lafayette campus. I’m skeptical. PUI students will be able to take in-person classes in Indy and online classes offered by Purdue faculty in West Lafayette. Eventually, PUI students may be allowed to commute an hour to West Lafayette to take in-person classes there, but not for at least a few years. But If I were to hazard a guess: The students at Purdue West Lafayette are significantly stronger than the students at Purdue Indianapolis, and that difference will persist for at least a decade. Purdue West Lafayette is known as a world-class engineering school. Purdue in Indianapolis is not. No matter how the university might protest otherwise, everyone still knows that the real Purdue is in West Lafayette. So West Lafayette is likely to attract a much stronger applicant pool than Indianapolis. The same dynamics will play out among the faculty as well—after the embarassing “university tenure” smoke clears—but I think that’s less significant. It’s the students, more than the faculty, that make Purdue such an engineering powerhouse. Well-taught university classes are calibrated to match the backgrounds and skills of the students that take them. If the Purdue West Lafayette faculty have stronger students on average, they will teach harder classes, because the students will demand them. If the Purdue Indianapolis faculty have weaker students on average, they will teach easier classes, because the students will require them. And that’s true even for classes that have identical catalog descriptions, identical advertised learning goals, identical textbooks, and even identical lectures. (Note well: “stronger” and “weaker” do not mean “smarter” and “dumber”, but rather “more prepared” and “less prepared”.) In the long run, the difference between the two Purdue campuses might even out, or even reverse, but I’m not holding my breath. tl;dr: More IUPUI, because that’s what PUI actually is.

Question: What are the fields of "computational algebraic geometry", "computational geometry", and "computational game theory" and what do they study?
Answer: Computational geometry is the study of algorithms and data structures for problems where the input has a natural interpretation as points, lines, planes, circles, spheres, line segments, polygons, axis-aligned boxes, or other simple (typically low-dimensional) geometric objects. Here are some typical problems: Computational geometry is primarily concerned with objects that have linear or piecewise-linear descriptions, such as polyhedra with flat faces. Computational algebraic geometry deals with geometric problems where the objects are best described with higher- (but still low-) degree polynomials. Problems of this form arise naturally in the study of (inverse) kinematics and visibility, even when the underlying physical objects are piecewise-linear. (Beware, this stuff gets really complex really quickly.) Algorithmic game theory is the study of algorithmic problems for competing strategic agents, for example, players in a game, bidders in an auction, candidates in an election, or children fighting over a birthday cake. Game theory does have some overlap with geometry—or more accurately topology—in the form of certain fixed-point theorems.

Question: Why is it true that mathematical logic, as is taught to graduate students today in pure math, can be taught to students in years 6-8 of pre-university education?
Answer: Before you ask why something is true, maybe you should confirm that it’s true. Here is the syllabus for a graduate-level course in mathematical logic at my university: Most 7th graders with strong math backgrounds and interest can be taught the basic syntax and mechanics of first-order predicate logic. (I actually played WFF-n-PROOF as a kid.) But the compactness theorem? Gödel’s completeness theorem? Morley’s categoricity theorem? The Löwenheim–Skolem theorem? The decidability of Presberger arithmetic? The undecidability of Peano arithmetic? Those are all standard ingredients of graduate-level logic courses, but unless you’re teaching a roomfull of Terry-Tao-class child prodigies, they’re completely out of reach of 13-year-olds.

Question: Im a doing my PhD in economics..My girlfriend's brother is a mathematician. She keeps saying that economics is not as hard as math and the ones who are doing PhD in economics are only doing it because they found math too hard. Is this a red flag?
Answer: Yes, your girlfriend’s habit of comparing you negatively to her brother is a red flag. Your girlfriend’s contention that all economists are failed mathematicians is not just false, but profoundly disrespectful. Skill in research mathematics is not a virtue. The conceit that mathematicians (or whoever) are smarter—and by implication better—than economists (or whoever) is toxic nonsense. Some people decide not to be mathematicians because they find mathematics less rewarding than some other pursuit. And some people decide not to be mathematicians because they’ve met too many asshole mathematicians, and they don’t want to hang out with assholes. Neither of these choices has anything to do with finding math too difficult. (This is not unique to mathematics; the same goes for every other vocation.)

Question: What do you think about UIUC MCS in the Chicago program? I saw your post mentioned that online MCS can not carry the prestige as on campus. How about the Mcs in Chicago?
Answer: I assume this question is referring to this answer of mine: The on-campus MCS program in Chicago is still brand new. The first cohort of admitted students started in January 2023, and we were only approved to begin admitting international students for Fall 2024. It’s too early to tell how successful the program will be, or how much prestige it carries relative to the on-campus MCS program in Urbana-Champaign. The MCS programs in Urbana and Chicago offer the same classes. Faculty teach live in one location, with lectures live-streamed or at least recorded for students at the other location. MCS students in both locations have a cohort of other students at the same location to work/study/network with—physically, in the same room—which removes one of the biggest disadvantages (in my opinion) of the online MCS program. But the two programs are different. The MCS program in Chicago is much smaller than the one in Urbana, which means (especially for courses taught in Urbana) it may be harder for Chicago students to get attention. There are significantly fewer faculty and TAs in Chicago, so Chicago students are more likely to interact with course staff online. To first approximation, Chicago students won’t be exposed to the amazing community of undergrads and PhD students and postdocs and faculty (other than their instructors) in Urbana-Champaign. I expect fewer recruiters to visit 200 South Wacker Drive than the Siebel Center; on the other hand, the Chicago students are already in Chicago. So which is better? If you’re the type of person who can’t live without the noise and hustle and diversity and options of a big city, you’ll be happier in Chicago. (There are no dinner cruises on Boneyard Creek.) If you want to complete the degree part-time while you work, there are more employment opportunities in Chicago. Otherwise, I’d recommend coming to Urbana. One final note: At least for now, students cannot freely move back and forth between Urbana and Chicago programs; you have to choose one location or the other when you apply. Classroom seats and advising staff are limited resources in both locations, so we need to allocate them carefully.

Question: Can I get accepted in an economic PhD if I have already done a biology PhD but not an economics undergraduate degree?
Answer: Probably not. You already have a PhD, so you already know how to do research—how to identify and read relevant literature, how to formulate a testable hypothesis, how to teach yourself unfamiliar concepts or techniques, how to “read the room” (by reading the literature) to understand whether your research problem is interesting, how to design and perform experiments, how to analyze data, how to learn how to write for your audience, how to respond to Referee #2, and so on. Yes, the specifics differ from one field to the next, but that’s just a matter of degree—the specifics also vary from one problem to the next. If you don’t have a strong enough economics background to succeed in an economics PhD program, then you won’t succeed in an economics PhD program. If you do have a strong enough economics background to succeed in an economics PhD program, you don’t need an economics PhD. Just start doing economics research.

Name: Jeff Erickson
Question: Should I try transferring into the computer science program at Carnegie Mellon after being admitted for statistics and machine learning, or is it impossible?
Answer: Did you apply to the computer science program? If you did, you’ve already been rejected. Do you have some compelling new information that would convince the admissions committee to change its mind? If you didn’t, then it looks like you played stupid games and you are about to win stupid prizes. If you really wanted to major in computer science, then you should have applied to study computer science. It looks like perhaps you intentionally applied to another less competitive program, in the hope of doing an end-run around admissions by transferring. If that was actually easier than being admitted directly into CS, everyone would do it. But, okay, yes, it is possible. You can go through a more competitive version of the standard admissions process: Meet regularly with the CS major’s CS Undergraduate Program Administrator. Earn an average grade of 3.6/4.0 (four As and two Bs) or better in the first six required (and challenging) CS classes. Then fill out the internal transfer request form, including a 1–2 page essay describing your interests and goals and purpose in transferring. And then maybe, if the class isn’t already full, and if you are extremely lucky, you might get in. But I wouldn’t count on it. The accounts I’ve read suggest that the number of internal transfer students is very very small; most CS majors would not qualify for transfer if they had not been admitted as first-year students. My department (ranked slightly below CMU) eventually decided to close our core CS major to internal transfers. There was just no fair way to choose the small number of transfer students we could support from the large number of highly qualified and motivated applicants, despite the high bar to even be considered. CMU’s bar to even be considered is higher than ours was. tl;dr: If you really want to major in computer science, and you’ve been admitted to the computer science major somewhere else, go there.

Question: I'm a student who's been accepted at UIUC and NYU for engineering, and I'm having trouble choosing. What is the career placement like at UIUC, and is the quality of their program as good as its ranking indicates?
Answer: First, see Shane Ryoo's excellent answer, especially this point: Your career outcomes can vary wildly. The school is not going to be your limiting factor. Shane was a student at Illinois; let me give a complementary perspective as a faculty member. Yes, the quality of our undergraduate engineering programs is as at least as good as our rankings indicate. Career placement from Illinois is fantastic; here is a snippet from the university’s 2021–22 annual outcomes report. But if you are trying to choose between Illinois and NYU, I honestly think you are asking the wrong question. Here is the question you should be asking: Would I be happier attending a commuter campus in New York City, or attending a more traditional large state university in a college town? If you are the type of person who thrives on the noise and crowds and hustle and culture and variety and novelty and excitement and frustration that comes from living in a big city, you are going to be absolutely miserable in Champaign-Urbana. And if you are miserable, the quality of the educational programs that Illinois offers will not matter one bit, because miserable people do not perform to their own potential. See my previous answer to a closely related question: If possible, visit both campuses in person. Talk with current students and alumni — not just tour guides — from both universities. Do a serious search at both locations for the kind of culture you want, the kind of housing you want, the kind of food you want, the kind of commute you want, the kind of social life you want, the kind of college experience you want. You can [launch a successful career] from either of these universities, if you do well and you take advantage of the opportunities that each university offers. Your future success depends far more on you than it does on where you get your degree. But if you put yourself into an environment that you can’t tolerate, you won’t be as successful.

Question: When publishing in an IEEE journal, it is required that the research is novel. Please consider that my research was conducted before, but mine enhances the field in numerous aspects. Is novelty looked for in the title or the abstract of the research?
Answer: Journals (through their editors and referees) look for novelty in the content of the paper. The title and the abstract are just window-dressing. If your research “enhances the field in numerous aspects”, then it is your job as the author to convince the reader (represented by their proxies: the journal editor and the referees) that your “enhancements” are interesting, significant, and novel. That must be the entire point of your paper. Those enhancements are your research.

Question: I am currently a PhD student at the University of Michigan - Dearborn. Is there any opportunity for me to transfer to study at the main campus, University of Michigan - Ann Arbor?
Answer: There is no such thing as “transferring” from one PhD program to another. Even if you accepted admission to the PhD program in Ann Arbor, you would be starting your PhD over from scratch (possibly except for a few classes). If you all want to do is study in Ann Arbor, all you need to do is (1) drive to Ann Arbor and then (2) study. It’s very likely that the University of Michigan system shares library privileges between campuses, and there are coffee shops and Google everywhere. If you what you really want is to work with faculty at Ann Arbor, you can do certainly that, exactly the same way that you would work with faculty in East Lansing or Madison or Austin or Münich—networking. Go to conferences in your chosen field of study. Drive to Ann Arbor (or join a Zoom broadcast) and attend seminars in your subfield; volunteer to give a talk; give a really good talk. Ask your PhD advisor to introduce you to colleagues that share your research interests. If a research collaboration naturally evolves, congratulations! (Do not attempt to do this without the support of your PhD advisor in Dearborn.) If what you really want is a PhD from UM Ann Arbor, the only way to get that is to apply and to be admitted, just like you were at Dearborn, and then do the work, just like you’re doing at Dearborn.

Question: What are some good passion projects for a high school student who wants to major in Computer Science and is interested in machine learning? Does anyone have a passion project that got them into a prestigious university for CS?
Answer: A passion project will not “get you into” a prestigious university for CS. In particular, a passion project related to computing is neither necessary nor sufficient to get into a good university for CS. Roughly 25% of first-year CS majors in my department (consistently ranked #5 in the US) have zero previous programming experience. You do need stellar grades, especially in STEM courses, especially in math. You do need a thoughtful, well-written application statement. It’s helpful to have extracurricular activities that display your honest interests, independence, and maturity, but those interests do not have to be related to computing. In other words: Pursue a passion project because it’s something you’re honestly passionate about, not because you think it’ll give you a leg up on the competition. There are lots of online courses and web sites with suggestions for projects related to machine learning, aimed at many different levels of skill/experience. Two random examples: Write a program to recognize the ASL alphabet[1][2][3]or identify bird songs[4][5][6]. (But I wouldn’t recommend those examples if you don’t already care about sign language or birds.)

Question: If I'm on the waitlist of a PhD program and I checked the box for master's as well, does it mean that they will most likely accept me for a master’s if they reject my PhD application?
Answer: If you receive a formal letter from the department offering you admission to the PhD program, then you have been admitted to their PhD program. If you receive a formal letter from the department offering you admission to the master’s program, then you have been admitted to their master’s program. If you receive a formal letter from the department stating that you will not be offered admission to the PhD program, then you have been rejected from the PhD program. If you receive a formal letter from the department stating that you will not be offered admission to the master’s program, then you have been rejected from the master’s program. If you have not received one of those four letters, the only thing you can conclude is that you have not been admitted yet.

Question: What is the maximum length of a substring that occurs twice in a given string?
Answer: That depends on the given string, obviously. The maximum answer over all strings of length n is exactly n − 1 . For example, the string AAAAAA occurs exactly twice as a substring of AAAAAAA. The minimum answer over all strings of length n is exactly 0. The empty string is the only string that appears more than once as a substring of STRING.

Question: What could be the cost of a PhD in CS?
Answer: The cost to the student should be negative. Any department that really wants you will guarantee multiple years of funding, including a tuition waiver and a modest stipend, for as long as you are making steady progress toward your degree. Paying for a PhD, especially in computer science, is stupid. The cost to the university? That’s a little harder to quantify, but I’ll give it a shot. Let’s assume a student that takes six years (twelve semesters) to complete their degree. The student is supported for each of those 12 semesters by either a research assistantship (typically paid from a faculty member’s research grant) or a teaching assistantship (typically paid from the department’s education budget). Let’s assume one summer with an RAship and the other four summers with industry internships (which cost the university nothing). The main direct expense comes from the assistantships. In my department, a 9-month 20-hour-per-week RAship pays about $30,000 per year to the student before taxes. Considering tuition, health insurance, and other benefits roughly doubles that cost. Six years of 9-month RAship, plus another 3-month RAship for one summer, comes to just less than $400,000. The student is likely to have a few other smaller expenses covered by their advisor’s grants, like a laptop and a few conference trips, or by general university funds, like power, internet, and working bathrooms. Let’s generously call that another $20,000. In other words, noise. Then we have expenses that are harder to quantify. How much of the advisor’s salary do you consider part of the cost of one PhD student? Include faculty time spent advising and/or directly collaborating with the student, as well as prorated time to write grant proposals to fund the student. These times vary wildly between different students and different advisors, but let’s make a ball-park guesstimate of 10% of the advisor’s time per student. Assuming the professor makes $150,000 per year (typical for a mid-career associate professor in my department) plus benefits, that’s conservatively another $100,000. There are a huge number of other faculty, staff, and administrators whose work is also crucial for the PhD student’s success: The instructors of the classes they TA, other faculty collaborators, the staff who process assistantship paperwork every semester, the advisor’s clerical assistant, various sysadmins and janitors and associate department chairs. But these costs are relatively small per student. tl:dr: Each computer science PhD student in the US costs their university about $500,000.

Question: How can I find the time complexity of this recursive function using master’s theorem, T(n) = 2^nT(n/2) + n^n?
Answer: The problematically-named Master Theorem describes how to solve certain recurrences of the form T ( n ) = a T ( n / b ) + f ( n ) , where a and b are constants—explicit numbers that you can write down and that do not depend on the variable n . The expression 2 n is not a constant; it is a function of n . So the Master Theorem doesn’t say anything directly about this recurrence. So we have to transform the recurrence into a form where the Master Theorem applies. Consider a new function T ′ ( n ) = T ( n ) / 4 n . Plugging this definition into our given recurrence gives us a simpler recurrence for T ′ ( n ) : T ′ ( n ) = T ( n ) / 4 n = ( 2 n T ( n / 2 ) + n n ) / 4 n = T ( n / 2 ) / 4 n / 2 + ( n / 4 ) n = T ′ ( n / 2 ) + ( n / 4 ) n The simpler recurrence T ′ ( n ) = T ′ ( n / 2 ) + ( n / 4 ) n has precisely the form required for the Master Theorem, with the constants a = 1 and b = 2 . You can take it from here.

Question: How does UIUC MS CS's admission process work? Some people say if you're not interviewed, you're rejected. Some say it is not the case. Is the decision dependent on the adcom or profs are also involved?
Answer: “Interviewed”? We interview master’s applicants? That’s news to me. The only interviews I’m aware of for graduate applicants are about language proficiency, in cases where the applicant’s TOEFL speak score is below 24. It’s entirely possible that some individual professors may interview prospective master’s students for other reasons, but I wouldn’t know—we are a huge department, far too big for me to know everyone. Formally, all admissions decisions are made by the admissions committee. In practice, a strong endorsement from a single faculty member carries a lot of weight, as long as the applicant is superficially qualified. Faculty have access to the complete applications database, and any faculty member is welcome to comment either positively or negatively on any application. Admission requires at least one faculty member to indicate their willingness to advise.

Name: Jeff Erickson
Question: How do you write a perfect SOP for the USA?
Answer: You don’t. Perfection is impossible. First, describe your reasons for attending your target degree program. What are your academic/research interests? What are your career goals? Be honest, credible, and specific. As much as possible, write in the idiomatic language of someone who is already successful in your chosen career, in your target field. In particular, if you are applying for a research degree, describe your specific research interests using the technical language of successful researchers with the same interests. (This is impossible unless you actually have research interests.) Second, provide concrete evidence that is not already obvious from your academic record that you are likely to succeed in your target degree program. Throw any platitudes about “passion” and “changing the world” and “since my first trembling steps” into the fire—wanting to succeed is not evidence that you are likely to succeed. Tell us what you’ve actually done. In particular, tell us what you’ve actually done that is related to your specific research interests. Tell us why this program is a good match for your goals and interests. Be honest, credible, and specific. As much as possible, write in the idiomatic language of someone who is already successful in your chosen career, in your target field.

Question: With the AI boom, there has been a big spurt in research papers and PhDs. DL papers give a sense of empirical engineering. With such environment, do you still see the same value in a PhD?
Answer: Of course I do. In the middle of the 19th century, there was a gold rush in California. Gold was plentiful enough that prospectors could barely scratch out a living hanging out at a creek, carefully swishing silt and pebbles in a pan, and fishing out little nuggets of gold. Occasionally some very lucky prospectors found larger deposits—either in the ground or in other prospectors’ bags—and either became extremely rich or murder victims. Question: Is it true that while solutions to quintic equations can be expressed in radicals, they can't be expressed using finitely many radicals and require infinitely many of them?
Answer: Yes, it is true. On the one hand, the Abel-Ruffini theorem implies that for any integer d ≥ 5 , there are polynomials of degree d whose roots cannot be written as closed-form algebraic expressions. Closed-form expressions are finite by definition. On the other hand, a 2014 paper of Nikos Bagis shows that the roots of any polynomial of degree 5 or 6 can be written using infinite periodic sequences of nested radicals. See also this Math Stack Exchange question.

Question: What is the Big-O notation of the following nested loop: for (int I=0; I<n; I++) {for (int j=I+1; j<n; j++) {…}}?
Answer: That depends on what’s inside the innermost block “{…}”. Consider the following examples: This algorithm runs in O ( n 2 ) time. The outer loop executes n times; for each iteration of the outer loop, the inner loop iterates at most n times; and each iteration of the inner loop takes O ( 1 ) time. This algorithm runs in O ( n 3 ) time. The outermost loop executes n times; for each iteration of the outermost loop, the middle loop iterates at most n times; for each iteration of the middle loop, the innermost loop iterates at most n times; and each iteration of the innermost loop takes O ( 1 ) time. This algorithm runs in O ( n 2 log n ) time. The outermost loop executes n times; for each iteration of the outermost loop, the middle loop iterates at most n times; for each iteration of the middle loop, the innermost loop iterates at most log 2 n times; and each iteration of the innermost loop takes O ( 1 ) time. This algorithm runs in O ( n log n ) time. The outer loop executes n times; for each iteration of the outer loop, the inner loop iterates at most log 2 n times (because the body of the loop changes the loop index); and each iteration of the innermost loop takes O ( 1 ) time. This algorithm runs in O ( n ) time. In each of the n iterations of the outer loop, the inner loop iterates only once. Even more extreme: This algorithm runs in O ( 1 ) time. For the next two examples, suppose the function TowerOfHanoi(n) prints a solution to the Tower of Hanoi problem with n disks (moving from peg 1 to peg 2), in O ( 2 n ) time. This algorithm runs in O ( n 2 n ) time. The outer loop iterates n times, and for each iteration of the outer loop, the inner loop spends at most ∑ j < n O ( 2 j ) = O ( 2 n ) time calling TowerOfHanoi. This algorithm runs in O ( 2 n ) time. The outer loop iterates n times. During the i th iteration of the outer loop, the inner loop spends at most ∑ k < n − i O ( 2 k ) = O ( 2 n − i ) time calling TowerOfHanoi. So the total running time is at most ∑ i < n O ( 2 n − i ) = O ( 2 n ) . Finally: This algorithm never halts; it just Yo!s forever.

Question: How do we build a habit of daily book reading?
Answer: Read from a book every day. Specifically, commit to sitting down with a book every single day and reading at least one page. (You can increase the number of pages later; your first step is to establish the habit of reading at all.) Pick a book to read that you actually enjoy reading! If you like historical biographies, don’t pick up a Harlequin romance or a physics textbook. It may be helpful to set aside a specific time every day where reading is your absolute first priority—not work, not shopping, not cleaning, not talking with friends, not paying bills, not driving kids around, not Skyrim—reading. (I recommend making an exception for medical emergencies.) It may be also helpful to keep a record of your progress: Keep a journal of how many pages you read from which book each day, or just mark a calendar every day that you read. It may also be helpful to have a reading partner or group, who you either read with at the same time, or check in with every few days. Finally, be gentle with yourself. You will miss a day here and there—you are, after all, human—and that is really completely okay. Remember that your goal is improvement, not perfection.

Question: What do I do if I am stuck on a problem and after spending a long time still cannot solve the problem myself or verify that my solution is correct? I may not find the solution anywhere and feel I do not learn much if I cannot check my work.
Answer: Wait, which is it? You cannot solve the problem, or you cannot verify your solution? It can’t be both. Do you have a tentative solution or not? If you do have a tentative solution, you must have come up with it somehow. If it just appeared to you fully formed, like Athena from the forehead of Zeus, it’s probably (but only probably) a fantasy, too good to be true. Similarly, if you download your potential solution from the internet, then well, you’re on your own; not doing the work yourself to derive the solution is going to make the solution much much harder to verify. But if you derived your tentative solution methodically, piece by piece, you have an opportunity to check your work methodically, piece by piece. Can you prove that the first step you took toward your tentative solution is correct? What made you confident enough in your first step to take a second? If you do not have a solution, are you at least making progress toward a solution? Do you have a rough outline of what a solution should look like? Have you solved any special cases? Have you solved any closely related problems? What happens when you change that constant 2024 to 3, or 2, or 1, or even 0? Can you express (not solve, just describe) the problem using more formal mathematics? Is this really a problem about linear equations, or equilibrium of forces, or related rates, or spanning trees, or martingales? Can you express (not solve, just describe) the problem geometrically? Or are you naïvely expecting the solution to appear fully-formed, like Athena from the forehead of Zeus? Are you really working toward a solution, or are you trying to prove that you are clever? If this is a homework problem: Do you understand the relevant portions of the textbook? Well enough to teach them to other people? Have you been going to lecture? To your discussion/recitation/lab section? To office hours? Are you asking questions? If not, why not? If so, are your questions closer to “What is the solution?” (bad) or “How should I approach this?” (good). If this is a research problem: Do you understand the relevant portions of the research literature? Well enough to teach them to other people? Have you tried applying the techniques (not tweaking the solutions) in the papers you’ve read? Are you regularly discussing your progress with your advisor, or with other colleagues? If not, why not? (No, you don’t need a solo paper.) Are you sure you’re trying to solve the correct problem? Have you at least carefully written up the parts that you are sure about? In all cases: What have you tried that didn’t work? Why didn’t it work? What did you learn from the realization that it didn’t work?

Question: Is it true or false? Any algorithm for sorting an array of size n must make at least Ω (n log n) comparisons.
Answer: FALSE. Any sorting algorithm that relies solely on comparisons must make at least Ω(n log n) comparisons in the worst case. More generally, any sorting algorithm that can be modeled as a family of bounded-degree decision trees (or as a family of algebraic computation trees) requires at least Ω(n log n) operations in the worst case. But there are sorting algorithms that do not rely on comparisons (or other bounded-degree branches, or algebra) at all. The simplest of these algorithms is counting sort, which performs ZERO comparisons. Counting sort also runs in O(n) time, assuming we’re working in a model of computation that allows reading and writing input numbers in O(1) time. (If you’re not comfortable with that assumption, you’re going to have to work hard to justify comparing two input numbers in O(1) time.) Counting sort cannot be modeled as a bounded-degree decision tree, because it directly uses the data being sorted as indices into an array. If we work in the standard word RAM model, it is possible to sort n integers, each of which fits in a w-bit word, in O(nw) time using radix sort, or in O(n log w) time using van Emde Boas trees or fusion trees, or in O(n log log n) time using a complex algorithm of Yijie Han, or even in O(n) time if the word size w is sufficiently large. None of these algorithms work by performing one comparison at a time; the more efficient algorithms pack multiple integers into a single word, so that multiple comparisons can be performed in parallel using a single subtraction. The phrase “in the worst case” is also crucial; many sorting algorithms are faster when the input array is almost sorted. For example, if the index of each each element in the input array differs from its index in the output array by at most 10, then bubble sort ends after at most 10 passes, and thus sorts the array in only O(n) time.

Question: Is there any algorithm to count number of non_empty sub sequence of an array with integer average, expect the brute force way? Any DP solution?
Answer: First, I’m going to assume that the input is an array of integers. Otherwise, the is no hope of doing anything subexponential. (This is a perfectly sensible question to ask about arrays of rational numbers, or floating point numbers, or even (depending on your religion) real numbers.) Do you mean the number of subsequences with a given integer average, or the number of subsequences with arbitrary integer averages? Which of the following sentences is an example solution to your problem? The given-integer problem is a generalization of the classical Subset Sum problem: Given a set S of n integers and a target sum T, does any subset of S sum to exactly T? This was one of the first problems that Richard Karp proved NP-hard in 1972. However, there are several algorithms that solve Subset Sum faster than brute force. Both of these algorithms can be adapted to solve your subsequence-counting problem, with the same running time. The arbtirary-integer problem is a bit more interesting. Offhand, the fastest algorithm I’ve found is a dynamic programming algorithm that runs in O ( n 5 ) time, whose subproblems are described by the following function. Suppose the input array is A [ 1.. n ] . For all integers 0 ≤ i ≤ n and 0 ≤ ℓ ≤ n and 1 ≤ m ≤ n and 0 ≤ r < m , let NSSM ( i , ℓ , m , r ) denote the Number of Subsequences of the prefix A [ 1.. i ] of length ℓ whose Sum Modulo m is equal to r . We need to compute ∑ ℓ NSSM ( n , ℓ , ℓ , 0 ) . The NSSM function satisfies the following recurrence. The second base case uses Iverson brackets. The main recursive case adds the number of subsequences that contain A [ i ] to the number subsequences that omit A [ i ] . NSSM ( i , ℓ , m , r ) = ⎧ ⎪ ⎪ ⎪ ⎪ ⎨ ⎪ ⎪ ⎪ ⎪ ⎩ 0 if  i < ℓ [ r = ∑ i j = 1 A [ j ] mod m ] if  i = ℓ NSSM ( i − 1 , ℓ − 1 , m , ( r − A [ i ] ) mod m ) + NSSM ( i − 1 , ℓ , m , r ) otherwise This recurrence can be memoized into a four-dimensional array and evaluated for all arguments with four nested for-loops in O ( n 4 ) additions. (I’ll let you figure out the correct nesting order.) Each array entry NSSM [ i , ℓ , m , r ] is trivially at most 2 n , and thus can be stored in at most n bits, so each addition takes at most O ( n ) time. We conclude that the overall running time is at most O ( n 5 ) . (Integer precision issues are unavoidable here. If A [ i ] = 1 for all i , the correct output is 2 n . Notice that NSSM ( i , ℓ , 1 , 0 ) is the binomial coefficient ( i ℓ ) !) I’m absolutely sure this is not the fastest algorithm for this problem, but at least it answers your question. Yes, there is a dynamic programming algorithm.

Question: I have found an unintentional mistake in my published paper, which is exactly the same in my PhD thesis. What will be its consequence if I cannot tell my advisor about this mistake?
Answer: Been there, done that, three weeks before my thesis deposit deadline. My PhD thesis suddenly became 15% shorter, and my advisor and I published an erratum. In retrospect, it was a pretty stupid error, even though it had already survived several rounds of peer review. Because of this error, the following results have incorrect proofs in [1]: Lemma 3.1, Theorem 3.2, Theorem 3.3, Theorem 4.2, Corollary 4.3, Theorem 5.2, Theorem 5.3, Theorem 5.6, and Corollary 5.7. Correct (and much simpler) proofs of all but one of these results appear in [3]. You not only can tell your advisor, you must tell your advisor. Hopefully the mistake is straightforward to correct with an erratum to the journal. If your thesis is already deposited, there isn’t a good way to correct the official version, but you’re not going to lose your PhD degree. If your thesis is also available in a different form, such as a technical report or an arXiv preprint. you can publish a revision; you can also revise the version that you (and your advisor) publish from your own web page(s). The only potentially dangerous situation is if the mistake invalidates a significant fraction of your results (like mine did) and you haven’t defended/deposited your thesis yet (like I hadn’t) and you don’t have other independent work that still supports the same or similar conclusions (like, fortunately, I did). In this case, you need to publish a retraction, not just a correction, and you need to have a discussion with your advisor (and possibly the rest of your thesis committee) about the effect this necessary retraction will have on your dissertation. Norman Sleep’s answer is exactly right. It is far better to publish the correction or retraction yourself before someone else inevitably finds your mistake and label you either incompetent or unethical.

Question: You have n wine bottles, 1 of which is poisoned. You want to determine which bottle is poisoned by feeding the wine to the rats. The poisoned wine takes 1 hour to work. Given x hours, what is the fewest # of rats you need to find the poisoned bottle?
Answer: Given the stated conditions, I need exactly one rat. Moreover, I can complete the test in time arbitrarily close to one hour, provided I have a sufficiently accurate clock. Suppose we start the experiment precisely at noon. Suppose we give the rat a sample from every bottle, one at a time, at a rate of one bottle per second. That is, for each index k from 1 to n , we give the rat a sample of the wine from the k th bottle at exactly k seconds after noon. Then bottle k is poisoned if and only if the rat dies exactly k seconds after 1:00pm. The experiment is complete after at most 1 + n / 3600 hours. To complete the experiment within x hours, we need to sample the bottles at a rate of n / ( x − 1 ) per hour instead of one per second. Otherwise the experiment is unchanged. This is obviously not the intended solution; for that I defer to Roman Andronov’s lovely description. But notice that the intended solution allows—indeed, requires—wine from a large fraction of the bottles to be mixed before feeding them to the rats. So an arbitrarily small sample of the poisoned wine must kill the rat after one hour. If mixing arbitrarily small amounts of wine from multiple bottles before consumption doesn’t change the time for the poison to take effect, then why should mixing arbitrarily small amounts of wine from multiple bottles after consumption change the time for the poison to take effect? I’ve clearly violated the spirit of the puzzle, but what rule have I actually broken?

Question: Do acceptance rates differ depending on the program you are applying to?
Answer: Absolutely. Would you like some data? I have data. The University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign had an overall acceptance rate of 43.7% for first-time undergraduate admission in Fall 2023, but admission rates differed significantly by college, from a low of 21.6% for the School of Information Sciences to a high of 56.5% for the College of Agricultural, Consumer & Environmental Sciences [1]. Within the College of Engineering, which has an overall acceptance rate in the low 20%s, almost all new undergraduates are accepted directly into a specific major; I don’t believe this is true within any other college at Illinois. Acceptance rates vary dramatically by major. Among in-state applicants for Fall 2022 first-time undergraduate admissions, for example, computer science accepted 14%, while materials science accepted 71% [2]. Admission rates can vary even within specific disciplines. Illinois has sixteen undergraduate computer science majors. The most popular is the “Pure CS” (or as I prefer to call it, “Mere CS”) major in the College of Engineering, which had a Fall 2023 acceptance rate of 7.5% [1]. The others are blended majors marketed under the umbrella “CS+X”; these had an overall Fall 2023 acceptance rate of 19.6% [1]. The University doesn’t release major-specific statistics, but some of these blended majors (like Statistics & Computer Science and CS+Economics) are considerably more popular than others (like CS+Crop Sciences), so I’d be shocked if their acceptance rates were not significantly lower (and not just because they’re formally in different colleges). [1] Undergraduate Admissions: Admit Rates. Published by the University of Illinois Office of Undergraduate Admissions, October 2023. [2] UIUC Engineering acceptance rates by major and demographics, Reddit /r/ApplyingToCollege, April 2023.

Question: College professors – What have you seen undergraduate students do that they seem to think will impress you, but in actuality what they do does not impress you at all (maybe what they do even makes you think negatively of them)?
Answer: Having a 4.0 GPA I’m much more impressed by students who work outside their comfort zone, who take harder classes and/or engage more deeply with the material and/or work on interesting independent projects, even if that might negatively impact their GPA. Creative failure is much more interesting than merely ticking all the boxes. Grinding through ALL the problems In my algorithms classes, I regularly give out long lists of study problems before exams, on the order of 20 pages of problem statements. Over the years it’s become increasingly common for students to spend days before each exam grinding through Every. Single. Problem. in these lists, to make sure that they will recognize any similar problem if it appears on the exam. These students miss the point that I can come up with an unbounded number of new problems, which can be solved using the same process as the study problems, even if they don’t look like any study problem, and it’s really the process that I’m trying to teach, and therefore test. I’m not testing their ability to remember algorithms; I’m testing their ability to reason out algorithms on the fly. Also, four hours of sleep would do them more good than four more hours of studying the night before the exam.

Name: Jeff Erickson
Question: In the Statement of purpose, is it bad to mention your past work that motivated you to apply for the graduate program, even if you were not successful in achieving anything in that task? And simply stating what I did.
Answer: Absolutely not. Exactly the opposite. Research is not always successful. (If we knew in advance that a new research project would eventually be successful, it wouldn’t be research; it would just be homework.) Most ideas are bad. Some bad ideas look good at first, and we only realize they’re bad ideas when we put in the legwork to evaluate them carefully. Failure in research is not an option; it’s a requirement. So one of the most important habits for researchers to learn is to treat confusion, frustration, and failure as motivation, rather than discouragement. Showing off your good-faith research efforts even when they failed is strong evidence that you are learning this habit. Past research didn’t go well and you’re still eager to do it. Past research didn’t go well and you’re still eager to talk about what you did, and what went wrong. That’s a powerful signal of your research potential.

Name: Jeff Erickson
Question: Is it better to write a technical book instead of several research papers?
Answer: [A2A] Answering as a computer science professor: Not if you want tenure! The standard expectations for hiring and promoting faculty in most (if not all) fields of science and engineering include publishing research papers in peer-reviewed venues. In most fields that means refereed journals; in most subfields of computer science, that means competitive peer-reviewed conference proceedings. These venues are where the research community expect to see research results; publishing in these values is the easiest way to build both a public record of your research accomplishments and your reputation as a researcher. (Expectations in other disciplines are different, especially in the humanities.) It’s the easiest way not because it’s easy, but because that’s how everybody expects it to be done, so that’s where everyone’s attention already is. Hiring committees are going to look first at your publication record. Promotion committees are going to look first at your publication record. The people writing evaluation letters for your promotion case are going to look first at your publication record. Rule Number One in dealing with committees that might evaluate you for anything: Thou Shalt Not Give the Committee an Excuse to Think. Publishing a book instead of several papers is non-standard,.and doing anything nonstandard gives the hiring/promotions committee an Excuse to Think. You will be held to a more stringent standard, because people are generally skeptical about unfamiliar things, and [whining] thinking is haaaaaaard. Some committee members will just want to reflexively reject anything “weird”, so other committee members will have argue more strongly to convince them. Now, I’m not saying that it’s impossible to establish a strong enough reputation by writing a book to be hired and tenured. I’ve seen it work, but it’s rare. I don’t recommend the risk.

Question: What is the best way to write a research paper on the topic "design and analysis of a small modular reactor for remote and rural areas"? What exactly should it look like? What information is important to include for such research work?
Answer: Well, based on the title, I think you should proceed as follows: The precise content depends on your target audience. A paper written for a high school science teacher is a very different beast than a master’s thesis, or a patent application, or a paper written for a high-impact academic journal. Even for the same type of venue, expectations will vary by field. For example, I would expect a master’s thesis in civil engineering to be very different from a master’s thesis in electrical engineering or materials science or nuclear engineering, even with the exact same title and topic. The expectations of your target audience are best understood by reading other research papers on similar topics aimed at the same audience—many of which you’re likely to cite anyway—and by asking your research advisor / mentor / instructor.

Name: Jeff Erickson
Question: I am in my senior year of high school and failed a semester course. If my GPA from my 9-11 grade is a 3.6, how will an F on one semester affect my GPA?
Answer: For purposes of illustration, I’ll assume you took six classes every semester, that a single A– is worth 3.7, and in the first semester of your senior year, you got an A– in every class except the one you failed. You’re a high school senior, with (until recently) an A– average, so you should have absolutely no trouble repeating this calculation yourself, using your real grade data, to whatever precision you like. But this back of the envelope calculation should be enough to convince you that the effect of a single F on your overall GPA is insignificant. I suspect you’re really asking about the likely effect on college admissions. Yes, I think an F is likely to work against you. Many colleges only look at your GPA for the last few semesters; others, like the University of California system, use a custom GPA calculation. And the admissions committee isn’t just going to look at your GPA; they’re going to look at your actual transcript and see the F. That F indicates a major problem—something went badly wrong this semester. I expect the overall impact to be relatively minor, but that’s really just a guess. More importantly, the overall impact is completely out of your hands, and therefore not worth worrying about. Getting stressed about your F is not going to change its effects. Worrying about your F is not going to change its impact. Beating yourself up over your F is not going to change its impact. Anger, guilt, worry, and fear are all completely natural responses to failure, but they’re also completely unnecessary and unproductive. Attention, on the other hand, is productive, and may be necessary. The one thing you can do that will have the most positive impact in the long run is to address whatever issues led to that F. (Your earlier questions—assuming they were asked in good faith—suggest that you should (a) reduce your cannabis consumption and (b) find a safer place to live away from your abusive father.)

Name: Jeff Erickson
Question: Can applicants with a B+ undergraduate GPA increase their chances of acceptance to top 20 graduate schools by showcasing a publication, internships, and short work experience at NGOs?
Answer: I can only describe my experience at a top-5 department in computer science. Expectations in different fields are different, obviously. My department’s PhD program admits a small number of students with B+ undergrad GPAs every year. Not many, but some. Admissions committees for MS and PhD programs in computer science are looking primarily for evidence of your potential for research. Grades and test scores are extremely crude predictors of research ability; research is not just more homework. Applications from students with higher GPAs are more likely to get attention from faculty, but that’s really all your GPA is good for. Once your application is in front of faculty eyes, other features matter more. The most significant feature people look for is research experience. At one extreme, suppose you are a (co)author of a strong research publication in a top conference in your field, and you write coherently and convincingly about your results in your statement of purpose, and your letters of recommendation describe both the quality of your results and your specific contributions to those results—if you have all of that, then your grades won’t matter at all. After all, graduate school grades don’t matter, and you’re already acting like a successful graduate student. But very few applicants already have a strong publication record, or even publications of any kind. So there’s a tradeoff. Other types of research-ish experience — sub-coauthor research contributions, independent study projects, senior theses, participation in REU programs, graduate-level courses, open-source software projects, not-just-code-monkey internships, relevant (not-just-code-monkey) work experience, teaching experience, leadership in relevant student organizations, deep informal engagement with difficult course material, even just asking insightful questions in office hours — also carry significant weight, depending on how much they resemble parts of the process of doing high-quality research. tl;dr: The more your experience looks and sounds and smells like high-quality publishable research, the less your grades matter.

Name: Jeff Erickson
Question: ? Hey my love . Im in big problem 😞 could u help me / my professor wants from me to write a research composed of 20 pages 😞 I can’t do it . My topic is (speech community) please 😞 help me if u have a research about it or any thing?
Answer: Yes, you can. No, really. You can. Maybe not right away. Maybe not even by the time your professor’s assignment is due, but yes, you can write a 20-page research paper on “speech community”. The trick is to start by writing one page, or even one paragraph, or even just two sentences, about any topic. Write about literally anything. Get guidance and feedback from your professors, from your teaching assistants, from the writing/tutoring center if your school has one, or even from your peers. Watch your spelling and grammar and punctuation, and keep the emojis to a minimum 🙁. Stick to a single topic. Tell a story. That’s all writing is—telling a story. Once you’re more comfortable writing one page, write two. Once you’re more comfortable writing two pages, write five. Once you’re more comfortable writing five pages, write ten. Once you’re more comfortable writing ten pages, write twenty. Meanwhile, you also need practice learning to do research. Again, the best people to give you guidance and feedback are your teachers, your writing/tutoring center, and your librarians. Research involves a lot of reading, and a lot of taking notes and organizing information, but those are also skills that you can develop with practice. Learn a story about what you want to write about. That’s all research is—learning a story. But by far the most important thing about learning writing — or any other skill, like cooking, or dancing, or carpentry, or basketball, or interviewing for jobs, or flirting, or parenting — is that you have to do the work yourself. You have to try, you have to fail, you have to try again, you have to get help, you have to try again. The only way to learn to do the thing is to actually do the thing. Your other questions strongly suggest that you are taking a university-level class in linguistics. Since you’re taking a class that is asking for a 20-page research paper, you’ve already had opportunities to learn reading and writing and research skills, so you don’t need to start from scratch. And you were admitted based on your past academic record; the admissions committee was convinced that you can succeed at their university, if you take advantage of the opportunity to practice. Good luck!

Question: Is personality or quantitative background more important in a personal statement for CS Master's? I'm applying to programs for people without a CS background, but a quantitative one, and am unsure whether to emphasize quant proficiency or personality
Answer: The admissions committee is primarily going to look for evidence that you will succeed in their program. Instead of your personality or your quantitative proficiency. I recommend emphasizing what you’ve actually accomplished, especially accomplishments that are not already obvious from your grades and test scores, followed by what specific goals/opportunities motivate you to pursue a master’s degree in computer science. Your relevant accomplishments provide concrete evidence of your ability to succeed; your goals provide evidence of your motivation to succeed. Honestly, your personality is almost completely irrelevant, as long as you don’t come across as a vampire or a sociopath. And the admissions committee can get a fair idea of your quant proficiency from your transcripts and GRE scores.

Question: College professors often say that getting an A in their class is "not enough" for them to be able to write you a good letter of recommendation. What then is "enough"? In other words, what else should a student do to get a good letter?
Answer: The only person who can definitely answer this question is the professor. So how did the professor answer when you asked them this question? (You did ask them this question, didn’t you?) But I can guess: Something that convinces the professor that you would thrive in a graduate program. Something that makes you stand out from all the other students who got As. (I’m expecting to give A’s to about 100 of my 400 students this semester, and I’m one of the harshest graders in my department. I struggle to write recommendation letters for ten students per year; 100 is simply out of the question.) In particular, if you’re talking about recommendation letters for a research-based graduate program: Something that convinces the professor that you have the potential for high-quality independent research. Course grades are a very crude predictor of research potential, even when they’re not inflated. Classes are all about homework and exams. Research is not just more homework and exams. But one of the things they’re going to look for is initiative. And one good way to show initiative is to ask them directly “How do you decide whether to write a recommendation letter for someone?”

Question: A question to Computer Science faculty members, do you think that a faculty member with impressive research record is more capable of writing hard exam questions for undergrad courses than a faculty member with poor research record?

But more likely is not the same thing as more capable. I do find my own research experience helpful in coming up with good exam questions, but not as helpful as my many years of coming up with exam questions, and in any case, good questions are not the same thing as hard questions. And what about all those faculty with merely good research records?

Question: Is UIUC MSCS more competitive than their PhD program, considering both provide funding?
Answer: Here are some statistics about graduate applications in computer science at UIUC, for the Fall 2023 admissions cycle: Previous years’ application and admission rates are similar. So in terms of raw selectivity, yes, the MSCS program is more competitive. There are significantly more MSCS applicants than PhD applicants, and significantly fewer MCSC admission offers than PhD admission offers, so the admission rate for the MSCS program is significantly lower than for the PhD program. That doesn’t necessarily mean that your chances of admission would be significantly lower for the MSCS program than for the PhD program. First, a lot of self-selection goes into these applications; the application pools are different. Students who are less sure about liking research, or who are aiming at careers in industry, or who just don’t want to spend 5–7 more years in school are more likely to apply to the MSCS program. Second, the two programs look for different profiles of students; the admissions criteria are different. MS admissions are based more on coursework and potential for incremental research contributions in a relatively short time frame; PhD admissions are based more on potential to grow into a successful independent researcher over several years.

Question: While writing my SOP, to make a case in terms of why my proposed field is important, can I mention another paper's (preprint, not peer-reviewed) one small discussion that I felt was also relevant?
Answer: Is the preprint classified? Did the preprint come with a non-disclosure agreement? Is the “preprint” actually a journal submission for which you are a referee? Did you promise the author that you wouldn’t mention their work? Unless there’s some reason why you need to keep the preprint secret, then of course you can mention it in your statement. Moreover, if you are using ideas from that preprint, you must cite it. (Corollary: You cannot use ideas from papers that you are required to keep secret.) But I confess to being a little puzzled: Why do you need to make a case that your field is important? Statements of purpose are usually part of an application to graduate school. If the graduate school that you’re applying to doesn’t already think your proposed field is important, they’re a bad fit, and you shouldn’t apply there.

Question: Can I do a double major and a triple minor at the same time?
Answer: Mayyybe. But dear gods, why would you want to? Nobody but you, your parents, and possibly your significant other are going to be impressed with how many bureaucratic hurdles you jumped. That extra major and all those minors aren’t going to get you into a better graduate school or hired into a better job. Name: Jeff Erickson
Question: How do I finish my master's thesis, and how do I start?
Answer: If you don’t know how to start, it’s too early to worry about how to finish. Starting comes first. I recommend starting by understanding what a master’s thesis actually is—a document with your advisor’s signature on it. Sit down with your advisor and have an honest, detailed discussion of their expectations, and your department’s expectations, about suitable topics, length, rigor, novelty, formality, and so on. Ask for copies of a few successful master’s theses. The next step is to find a suitable research topic—something that sits at the intersection of your interests, your expertise, your advisor’s interests, and your advisor’s expertise. Some advisors will give you a narrow problem and insist that you do nothing else. Others will give you complete freedom to work on whatever you want. I tend to sit somewhere in the middle, suggesting a general area (within the bounds of my own expertise), but letting the student choose what specific problems to work on, with the goal of retroactively declaring whatever problem(s) they solve as the topic of the thesis. And then you start digging.

Question: Is it possible to take classes at a community/junior college as a way to potentially boost my GPA even though I already have a Bachelor’s degree? If so, how exactly does it work and could it help me into grad school?

Name: Jeff Erickson
Question: I failed the intro computer programming class in the first year, and I plan to retake it in the next semester. Will this impact negatively on my PhD application to the top grad schools?
Answer: Top grad schools in computer science? Slow your roll there, buddy. You’ve only taken one introductory programming class, and that didn’t go very well. What makes you think that you’ll be ready to go—or even want to—go to any graduate school, much less a “top” graduate school, in computer science? I’m not saying that a top CS graduate school is completely out of reach. I failed at least one class as an undergrad, and nearly failed several others, including courses that are directly related to my eventual research speciality. What I am saying is that you should focus on learning to crawl before you start planning to be the next Usain Bolt. Intro programming classes are weird rites of passage. When you’re a beginner, they can be incredibly difficult. Yeah, there’s new syntax to learn, but that’s not the actual hard part. The actual hard part is learning to think in a new way, rewiring your brain to deal with abstract concepts and conceptual frameworks that would have no evolutionary advantage on the savanna. (Easy: Tiger bad, climb tree, throw rock. Hard: Memory leak bad, chase null pointer, throw exception.) But after a few years of practice with the new brain wires, everything that’s taught in those introductory classes is a walk in the park—so easy that even a computer program as fundamentally stupid as ChatGPT can do them well. This is the easy stuff. Wait until you start designing algorithms, optimizing compilers, managing multiple levels of caches, securing databases, tweaking metaparameters, writing new programming languages, managing virtual distributed systems, dealing with millions of lines of code. You know. The fun stuff. All of that fun stuff depends on a rock-solid foundation that starts with the class you just failed. First retake the intro class and really master the material in it. Then take a few higher-level classes, so that you can start to see what computer science actually is, and really master the material in them. Then, if you like the material, and you find that you can do it well, start thinking about graduate school. (Note well: “Master the material” and “Do it well” are not synonyms for “Get an A.”) Graduate school in something else, like physics or linguistics? Just retake the class and do better; it’ll be fine.

Name: Jeff Erickson
Question: How should I deal with so many recommendation letters. I am applying for masters scholarships, and I am overwhelmed. Many scholarships require 1-3 recommendation letters. How should I get so many letters, from a few professors I know, any tips?
Answer: The way you get good recommendation letters for graduate school is by consistently acting like a successful future graduate student in front of faculty, so that they can write about how much you behave like a successful future graduate student. Successful graduate students talk with their professors outside of class; they ask probing questions about course material (and beyond) in class and in office hours; they actively hunt down independent study and research opportunities; they work on independent projects and show them off in public; they treat their professors as senior colleagues. So the students who get strong letters of recommendation letters for graduate school also do those things. I’m sure you already know this, but a single professor can write more than one recommendation letter, or more accurately, can write one recommendation letter and send it to multiple scholarships, fellowships, and graduate programs (perhaps with some light editing). So you need three letter-writers. Three. If you really consider three professors to to be “so many”, you haven’t been acting like a successful future graduate student.

Name: Jeff Erickson
Question: If logic gives meaning to the universe, how can scientific materialists explain the existence of the logical laws that govern it?
Answer: Pardon me, sir. What kind of dressing would you like on your word salad? Logic does not give meaning to the universe. The universe doesn’t have meaning, for the same reason that cats cannot be prime, or that black holes cannot vote for Trump. The universe isn’t even the kind of thing that can have meaning. You’re thinking of language. The universe is not a word, or a sentence, or a novel, or even an encyclopedia. Logical laws do not govern the universe. The universe is not governed by laws. The things we call “laws” in the context of science and mathematics are not the kinds of things that can be governed with. Scientific laws describe the universe, or more accurately, vastly simplified but useful models of the universe. Logical laws don’t even do that much, because logic isn’t about the universe at all; it’s about the language that we use to talk about the universe (or more accurately, our vastly simplified models thereof). De Morgan’s law says nothing about black holes or quantum entanglement. Protons don’t go to jail for violating modus ponens. Logic gives structure to the language that we use to talk about (models of) the universe. The laws of logic exist because we humans find them useful to talk about (models of) the universe.

Question: If I received a 91% on a paper worth 25% of grade and a 77% on the paper that is worth 30% of the final grade, what is my GPA thus far?
Answer: You don’t have a GPA yet. GPA is the average grade among all classes that you have completed. You haven’t completed this course, so you don’t have a course grade. The mapping between percentages and letter grades for your specific course should have been spelled out in the course syllabus.
