Question: Will I get accepted to UIUC engineering? I started my community college average, but I got my GPA to a 3.38. However, my academic rigor is high since I took around 30 credits in the spring, summer, and fall. I retook some, but also took hard classes.
Answer: A community college GPA of 3.38 almost certainly guarantees that you will not be admitted to the college of engineering at UIUC. The easiest way to get into Illinois Engineering from a community college is to already be enrolled in the Engineering Pathways Program. You have to apply for this program when you apply to the community college. Only a handful of community colleges in Illinois participate, but each one has specialized advisors to guide Pathways students into the right classes and to make sure they’re making adequate progress. After two years in the community college, Pathways students are then admitted to their chosen engineering major at Illinois, provided they have met the following requirements: The middle 50% of transfer students admitted to Engineering in Fall 2022 had GPAs in the range 3.78–4.00 [source]. Yes, that means more than 25% of admitted transfer students had perfect 4.00 GPAs. I believe these statistics include Pathways students, so the expected GPA for non-Pathways applicants is even higher. (Also, different majors have different admission rates, so for impacted majors like computer science or bioengineering, the average GPAs of successful transfer applicants are even higher.) Pathways or not, a GPA of 3.38 is just not competitive. Echoing Joshua Gross’s answer: You should look at other public universities in Illinois with egineering programs: UI Chicago, Illinois State, Southern Illinois at Carbondale, Southern Illinois at Edwardsville, or Northern Illinois. (Unfortunately, Illinois no longer participates in the Midwest Exchange Program, so public universities in nearby states aren’t going to be cheap.) (I am assuming, since you’re asking about UIUC, that you’re an Illinois resident. if you’re not an Illinois resident, everything I’ve written probably also applies to your state’s flagship public university, but not to its other public universities: Purdue but not IU Bloomington, UW Madison but not UW Milwaukee, and so on.)

Question: Will an online master’s in CS boost my application for a PhD?
Answer: Not in the top CS departments. Computer science PhD admissions committees are looking primarily for compelling evidence of research potential. Moreover, at top departments, admissions committees generally apply higher standards to applicants who already have graduate school experience of any kind, Instead of compelling evidence of research potential, we want to see compelling evidence of research success. Online master’s students have few if any opportunities to get involved in real (meaning “eventually publishable”) research. Sure, you may get more advanced classes, but classes are very poor predictors of research potential, especially at the graduate level. Research is not just more homework. So most online (and more generally course-based) masters students are digging themselves into a hole if they plan to pursue a PhD later. I can think of one exception to this guideline: You have a strong academic background in a different field, and you are pursuing an online master’s degree to build up your CS fundamentals. In that situation, the master’s degree is definitely helpful, but it will be difficult to get good recommendation letters from your online instructors (because, again, research isn’t homework). You should maintain connections with the faculty you interacted with as an undergrad, so that they can provide recommendation letters that talk more about your research potential. Anyone considering a PhD in computer science must read Mor Harchol-Balter’s advice on Applying to Ph.D. Programs in Computer Science. (The author is a professor at CMU, formerly a professor at MIT, and formerly a PhD student at Berkeley, with experience on the grad admissions committees at all three schools. Everything she writes is consistent with my own experience at Illinois.)

Question: Is it appropriate to email to the graduate program chair or coordinator, provide all my academic and professional background and inquire about my eligibility for the program?
Answer: Sure. But don’t expect to read it. If you’re lucky, they’ll send you a pointer to the web pages that describe their admission requirements and their application procedures. If you have a specific question that is not answered on the department’s web site, you’re far better off sending an email asking that specific question. For example, if one of the admission criteria is “an undergraduate degree in computer science or related field”, you might not be certain whether your degree is “related” enough for you to be eligible. But then you should ask that question directly: I am interested in applying to your graduate program, but I have an bachelor’s degree in Applied Eschatology from Miskatonic University, and I’m unsure whether that qualifies as a “related field” to computer science. What criteria do you use to decide whether a non-CS undergraduate degree is “related” enough to computer science to qualify for admission? On the other hand, maybe your real question is “Will I get in if I apply?” I’m sorry, but the graduate program chair doesn’t get to make that determination; that’s the job of the admissions committee. And the only reliable way to ask the admissions committee is by sending them a complete application.

Question: Why do we use the non-deterministic algorithm to solve an optimization problem?
Answer: First of all, there is more than one non-deterministic algorithm. So I think your question is asking “Why do we use non-deterministic algorithms to solve optimization problems?” And the answer is: We don’t! We use non-deterministic algorithms to prove theorems about optimization problems. Non-determinism is a mathematical abstraction. It is not a technique that one can actually use to solve optimization problems (or any other type of problem) in the real world.

Question: How can you justify that the non-deterministic algorithm is useful for solving the NP-hard optimization problem?
Answer: I don’t. Because it isn’t. Nondeterminism is a mathematical abstraction. Its utility is limited to proving mathematical theorems. It can’t be used to actually solve actual real-world instances of NPhard optimization problems, because truly nondeterministic computers—the kind that destroy their branch of the multiverse whenever something goes wrong—do not exist.

Question: Using Boolean, I’ve solved the Collatz conjecture, 3x3+1÷2=9.5. Where do I get my prize?
Answer: First you earn a PhD in mathematics, or some closely related field. Assuming you have a strong undergraduate math background, this should take you 5–6 years. After you earn your PhD, you publish your proof of the Collatz conjecture, in complete technical detail, in a mathematics research journal. A mathematics PhD isn’t normally necessary for publishing math research, but noboyd is going to want to read your supposed proof of the Collatz conjecture if you don’t at least have the minimal professional bona fides of a professional mathematician. There are just too many cranks out there, with too many bogus “proofs”. Finally, at least two years after publication, assuming the mathematics community judges that your proof is correct and you aren’t a member of a criminal organization, the Bakuage Co., Ltd., of Japan will give you a prize of 120 million Japanese yen, which at today’s exchange rates is worth about $800,000. Not bad for only a decade of work! I have no idea what “Boolean” is supposed to be (Boolean algebra?) or what the identity 3x3+1÷2=9.5 has to do with the Collatz conjecture.

Question: How likely am I to get into grad school if I had a 2.5gpa my first year? (only for one semester)
Answer: You haven’t given enough information to even guess at an answer. Your chances of getting into grad school depend on your entire cumulative academic record and whatever other evidence you can present that you will thrive in your target program, through your application statement and your recommendation letters. One bad semester is not going to kill your grad-school application if the rest of it is strong. In fact, low grades in early classes followed by higher grades in harder followup classes can tell a story about self-awareness, responsibility, and maturity that can actually improve your chances of admission.

Name: Jeff Erickson
Question: My supervisor keeps pushing me to do experiments, my chosen direction is about blockchain security, and I lose sleep over anxiety, I can't implement the article experiment.How do figure out a specific direction for a specific graduate thesis?
Answer: I lose sleep over anxiety This is a medical issue. Consult a doctor and/or therapist. Your health—including your mental health—is far more important than your PhD. And this point is far more important than anything else in my answer. I can't implement the article experiment. Why not? Do you not have enough time? (Then work with your advisor to develop a more reasonable schedule.) Do you not have the right expertise or technical background? (Then work with your advisor to develop the right expertise, or to choose a task that better exploits your existing expertise.) Do you find implementing other people’s experiments boring/pointless/frustrating? (Then work with your advisor to identify another task that better fits your interests.) Or is the pressure from your advisor to implement the experiments the problem? Then work with your advisor to reduce the pressure, or if that proves impossible, work with your department to identify another advisor. Hopefully you’re noticing a trend here. You need to talk with your advisor. You should be open, honest, and direct about your anxiety about these experiments, and ask for their help. It is literally their job to help you; that’s what the word “advisor” means. Meanwhile, the only person who can give you a more specific direction (within the scope of “blockchain security”) to pursue for your graduate thesis is you. Your advisor can offer suggestions, but ultimately, you have to make the decision about your degree. And yes, it’s possible that refusing your advisor’s suggestions might mean you need to find another advisor, but that was already true. If you and your advisor can’t converge on a specific topic that fits your expertise, your interests, your goals, and your mental health, then they are the wrong advisor for you.
